ideas.title: Trace-oxidant guard for amine laminates: ozone, NO2, formaldehyde and SO2 as a per-tonne fade term
ideas.one_line: A DAC bed processes about 3,200 mol of air per mol of CO2 captured, so ppb-level O3, NO2, HCHO and SO2 deliver about 3-4 mol of reactive molecules per tonne of CO2, the same order as the ~10 mol of amine nitrogen a sorbent can afford to spend per tonne. Measure the damage yield first. If it is at least about 0.05, fit an HVAC- or respirator-style chemisorptive guard (or spent sorbent) in front of the laminate.
ideas.mechanism: Every amine laminate is also an efficient scrubber of electrophilic and acidic trace gases. Ozone attacks C-H bonds next to nitrogen and starts radical chains. NO2 and SO2 form nitrate, nitrite and sulfite/sulfate salts that do not leave at 100 C (the heat-stable salts of flue-gas amine plants). Formaldehyde converts primary amines to imines and aminals. These gases arrive in proportion to the air processed, i.e. per tonne of CO2, not per cycle or per hour, so faster cycling cannot dilute the damage. Because reactive gases are removed in the first part of the channel, damage should show up as a poison front advancing from the air inlet. That matches the Climeworks/Svante DOE pilot autopsy (oxidation stronger on the air-inlet side) and would also explain why indoor lab tests with low ozone understate field fade. Imported fix: an inlet guard of the kind used in other sorbent families. Options are catalytic ozone decomposition on MnO2/hopcalite or activated carbon (aircraft ozone converters, HVAC chemical filters) plus alkaline or permanganate-impregnated media for SO2, NO2 and HCHO, which is the acid-gas pre-polishing that point-source amine plants use. A cheaper variant uses the main bed's own spent sorbent as a sacrificial front cartridge. A fully capacity-faded amine still reacts with these gases, and a 20,000-cycle life generates about 1.1 kg of spent sorbent per tonne CO2, which is about what a stoichiometric guard needs. The new quantity to measure is Y_cap, the mol of CO2 working capacity lost per mol of trace gas consumed.
ideas.key_parameters: Core unchanged (verifier reference): dH about -70 kJ/mol, dS about -165 J/mol/K, q_max 2 mol/kg, working capacity 1.04 mol/kg at 100 C and 1 kPa CO2, ideal heat 6.04 GJ/t; amine N about 9.3 mol/kg (40 wt% PEI); sorbent $20-50/kg. Trace gases (typical ranges, general knowledge, site-specific): O3 10-60 ppb outdoors and 5-15 indoors; NO2 2-30 ppb; HCHO 1-5 ppb outdoors and 15-40 indoors; SO2 1-5 ppb; H2S near geothermal plants such as Hellisheidi. Uptake coefficient gamma on the amine surface sets removal per pass. Damage yield Y_cap is the key unknown. Guard: 25-75 Pa added pressure drop; MnO2 or carbon for O3; K2CO3-, KOH- or KMnO4-impregnated alumina, or spent sorbent at about 3 mol/kg reactive, for acid gases and HCHO; replaced off-line.
ideas.quantitative_claims: All from g2_opus_ideas.py, run with the OptiLex verifiers. (1) At 420 ppm and 75% capture the bed processes 3,175 mol air per mol CO2 (1.76 million m3/t), so each ppb of a trace gas delivers 0.072 mol per tonne CO2: 40 ppb O3 gives 2.9 mol/t and a 55 ppb mixture gives 4.0 mol/t. A 20,000-cycle life consumes only 1.09 kg of sorbent, about 10 mol N, per tonne. (2) Fractional capacity loss per cycle = Y_cap x c/(x_CO2 x capture), i.e. 1.27e-4 x Y_cap at 40 ppb. Y_cap of 0.079 uses the entire 20%-over-20,000-cycles budget (1e-3 %/cycle); Y_cap of 0.28 alone matches the 3.5e-3 %/cycle implied by the Climeworks Gen 2 target. (3) TDA/GE measured 2.2e-3 %/cycle in lab air (500 ppm, 19% capture, 0.18 mol/kg); that whole fade is explained by Y_cap of only 0.04-0.08 if indoor trace gases total 25-55 ppb. (4) The published ozone upper bound (Jamdade, Cai, Sholl 2025: 0.0002 %/cycle, about 8% after 40,000 cycles) assumes 0.0040 mol O3 per cycle. That much air contains only 167 mol CO2, against the 552 mol the paper says was captured. Corrected for mass balance at 75% capture: 7.9e-4 %/cycle at 10 ppb (27% of sites after 40,000 cycles) and 3.2e-3 %/cycle at 40 ppb (72%), under the paper's own one-ozone-one-site assumption. (5) At Y=1 per N site, 40 ppb consumes 1.4% of bed N per 1,000 cycles, advancing from the inlet: 28% of the bed after 20,000 cycles. (6) Removal per pass in a 1 mm, 0.15 m laminate at 2 m/s is 12%, 69% and about 100% for gamma = 1e-5, 1e-4 and 1e-3. (7) The guard costs 0.07-0.22 GJ/t of fan work for 25-75 Pa ($1-3/t at $50/MWh), plus 0.36-1.1 kg/t of acid-gas media ($0-11/t; $0 with spent sorbent). (8) Value from the verifier (sorbent cost, wc 1.04): halving fade saves $24-56/t at $20/kg and $60-139/t at $50/kg, for starting fades of 2.2e-3 to 5.1e-3 %/cycle.
ideas.closest_known_work: Jamdade, Cai and Sholl, J. Phys. Chem. C 2025 (PMC11726669): DFT ozonolysis of mmen-Mg2(dobpdc), with a one-ozone-one-site upper bound of 0.0002 %/cycle that this idea finds under-counts the ozone dose about 4-fold. Zorrilla-Valtierra et al., Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2026: 8 h exposure to 50 ppm O3 plus NOx (about 57 ppb-years) lowered 400 ppm capacity of amine-MOF and PEI/MIL-101(Cr) composites. Rezaei and Jones 2013-14 on SO2/NO2 stability of supported amines in flue gas (from memory, not re-verified). Climeworks/Svante DOE pilot DE-FE0031952 autopsy: more oxidation on the air-inlet side. Flue-gas amine plants' SO2 polishing and NOx/nitrosamine control. A quick patent and literature search found no published test of an inlet guard on a DAC sorbent; patents were not searched exhaustively.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Fixed bed of 1 g PEI/silica (40 wt%), or Lewatit VP OC 1065, at 25 C and 50% RH, fed with zero-air plus 420 ppm CO2. Four arms: clean; plus 1 and 5 ppm O3 (two levels to check that damage scales with dose); plus 0.5-1 ppm NO2; plus 0.2-0.5 ppm HCHO. Run each arm until the delivered dose is about 2 mol per kg sorbent, roughly 15,000 plant cycles at 40 ppb; at 5 ppm and 2 L/min this takes about 3.5 days. Monitor inlet and outlet trace gas with a rented UV ozone photometer and NO2 and HCHO analysers. Measure CO2 working capacity by a 90 C N2 temperature-swing every day. At the end, cut the bed into 5 slices and measure capacity, N content and FTIR of each. Add a fifth arm with a MnO2/carbon plus alkaline-media guard upstream of the ozone arm. Pre-stated kill threshold: Y_cap below 0.01 for O3 AND below 0.02 for each of NO2, HCHO and SO2. At 40-55 ppb that means trace gases supply under about 15-25% of the 20,000-cycle fade budget, so the guard is not worth fitting. The idea is confirmed if Y_cap is at least 0.05 and capacity loss is concentrated in the inlet slice. Estimated cost $3-8k plus analyser rental, 2-4 weeks.
ideas.computational_test: Extend the verifier with a 1-D plug-flow laminate model that has trace-gas uptake (gamma) and site consumption, to predict the axial damage profile and fade per tonne for hourly O3, NO2 and HCHO records (EPA AQS or EEA) at real or planned plant sites, for example California, Louisiana, Iceland and Texas. Compare the predicted inlet-to-outlet damage ratio with the DOE pilot autopsy. Rank sites by expected trace-gas fade in $/t.
ideas.conventional_core: Steam/vacuum temperature-swing supported-amine laminate (Climeworks/Svante class: PEI/silica or benzylamine resin).
ideas.graft: An inlet chemisorptive or catalytic trace-gas guard, measured in other sorbent families: MnO2/hopcalite and carbon ozone decomposition in aircraft and HVAC filters, alkali- or permanganate-impregnated media from respirator, HVAC and fruit-store filtration, and SO2/NO2 pre-polishing ahead of flue-gas amine absorbers. Implemented cheaply as a sacrificial cartridge made from spent DAC sorbent.
ideas.why_different: It defines a third fade class: per tonne, alongside the per-cycle and per-hour classes the OptiLex map discusses. Neither faster cycling nor oxygen-free cool-down affects this class. It uses flux accounting rather than ppb-years, which shows that a contactor delivers about 81 m3 of air per kg per cycle, and it corrects the only published ozone bound by about 4x using mass balance. It also offers a falsifiable explanation of two existing anomalies, inlet-side oxidation and indoor-lab versus field fade, and reduces the question to one measured number, Y_cap.

ideas.title: Binderless powdered-resin precoat for moisture-swing capture (borrowed from condensate-polishing precoat filters)
ideas.one_line: Replace 0.6 mm moisture-swing resin beads with a 0.2 mm through-flow cake of commercial 20-60 um powdered anion resin on a fabric septum, as power-plant condensate polishers do. The measured 27-85 min intraparticle t90 falls to under a minute, so cycle time is set by air supply instead of diffusion, and the active layer can be replaced by back-pulse and re-precoat.
ideas.mechanism: Measured moisture-swing kinetics on quaternary-ammonium resins are limited by diffusion of water and ions inside 0.6 mm beads (LDF k 14e-4/s drying and 4.5e-4/s wetting, about 10x slower than process models assume). Sheets of powdered resin in polypropylene (Shi/Lackner 2017) were slowed by the binder (D 6.5e-12 m2/s; 31.8 min half-time at 100 um), and grafted mesoporous resins that are fast (2.9 min) carry only 0.26-0.28 mmol/g. Condensate polishing has long used finely ground bead resin (styrene-DVB, same chemistry, sold for its rapid kinetics) held without binder as a thin precoat on filter septa by the through-flow itself, then removed by back-pulse and re-applied. Applied to DAC: precoat the carbonate-form powdered anion resin at 0.12-0.18 kg/m2 on pleated PP/PET fabric. Pass ambient air through the cake at 8-20 mm/s, which is within normal pulse-jet baghouse air-to-cloth ratios, to dry it and load CO2. Then switch to a humid closed loop, or VMS-style water vapour, to release CO2. Because moisture swing is isothermal, the extra fabric and housing mass costs no heat. That is why this geometry suits moisture swing and not thermal swing. A field-degraded layer, such as the quaternary-ammonium loss seen outdoors over about 1,380 cycles, becomes a cheap powder swap rather than a bed replacement.
ideas.key_parameters: Resin: Type I or II quaternary-ammonium styrene-DVB (IRA-900 or A501 chemistry, or a commercial powdered anion grade), carbonate form, ion-exchange capacity about 2-4 meq/g. CO2 working capacity 0.9-1.27 mmol/g (400 ppm, 25 C, 20% RH dry step to 50-95% RH wet step; measured on beads). Water swing 17-24 mol H2O per mol CO2 in vapour mode. D_eff 2.8e-12 to 8.8e-12 m2/s, back-calculated from measured bead k. Particles 20-60 um (typical powdered-resin size, general knowledge). Cake 0.2-0.3 mm on fabric; face velocity 8-20 mm/s; cycles of 10-20 min dry plus 10-20 min humid; no regeneration heat. Product: 1-5 kPa CO2 in a humid loop, to be vacuum-compressed or passed to a second stage. Resin about $10-20/kg; lifetime unknown (outdoor beads fell to about 10% capacity after about 1,380 cycles, confounded by biofouling).
ideas.quantitative_claims: From g2_opus_ideas.py. (1) Scaling the measured bead k to 50 um particles gives k = 0.21/s for drying and 0.068/s for wetting (t90 0.18 and 0.57 min), versus 1.4e-3 and 4.5e-4/s (t90 27 and 85 min) for 614 um beads: about 150x faster. (2) A crude LDF cycle model with 0.9 mol/kg equilibrium swing gives 0.25-0.48 kg CO2/kg/day for beads (measured 0.19-0.27; VMS model 0.2-0.6). For a powder precoat it gives 1.4 kg/kg/day at 20+20 min and 2.9 at 10+10 min, with the full 0.9 mol/kg used per cycle. (3) Air needed is 77.7 m3 per mol CO2 at 75% capture, i.e. 52-129 L/s per kg resin at 10-20 min adsorption steps. A 0.2 mm cake of 50 um powder (0.12 kg/m2) then sees 7.8 mm/s (0.47 m/min), with a Kozeny-Carman cake pressure drop of 11 Pa plus fabric, or 0.03 GJ/t of fan work. A 0.5 mm cake gives 71 Pa (0.21 GJ/t). (4) Drying 17-24 mol water per mol CO2 from 20% to 60% RH at 25 C needs 1,360-1,920 mol air per mol CO2, less than the 3,175 mol needed to supply the CO2. Air drying capacity is therefore not the binding limit in vapour mode. (5) Latent heat of 17-24 GJ/t is supplied free by ambient air, but water consumption remains, and the product (1-5 kPa CO2, wet) still needs at least 0.26-0.32 GJ/t of ideal compression to reach 1 atm. (6) Sorbent cost from the verifier ($15/kg, 0.8 mol/kg): $309/t at 1,380 cycles and $28/t at 15,000 cycles. A one-year calendar life at 36 cycles/day is about 13,000 cycles, so if resin fade is time-based rather than cycle-based, fast cycling alone cuts sorbent cost about 10x.
ideas.closest_known_work: Shi, Lackner et al., PLoS ONE 2017: resin powder in polypropylene sheets, binder-limited, 31.8 min half-time. Wang et al., Sci. Rep. 2020: quaternised mesoporous resin, 2.9 min half-time but 0.26-0.28 mmol/g. Wang et al. 2017 kinetic analysis (PMC5480984): intraparticle diffusion controls, and the authors suggest smaller particles. Wang, Realff, Lively, ACS Sustain. Chem. Eng. 2025: IRA-900 beads limited by internal mass transfer. Sinyangwe, Wade et al. 2026 (VMS, measured k). Graver Powdex powdered resins for condensate-polishing precoat. Within OptiLex, pass 1 proposed thin reinforced AEM films and plasticised resins for the same kinetic bottleneck. No published binderless precoat moisture-swing test was found in a quick search.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Buy a commercial powdered strong-base anion resin, or grind and sieve IRA-900 or A501 to 38-75 um, and convert it to carbonate form. Precoat 0.2-0.3 mm onto a 5 cm2 PP or PET fabric disc in a through-flow cell. Cycle 400 ppm air at 20% RH (10 min) against humid N2 or a closed humid loop at 90-95% RH (10 min) at 25 C, with an NDIR CO2 analyser and a humidity sensor. Measure drying and wetting LDF k, CO2 released per gram per cycle, pressure drop at 10 mm/s, and cake retention over 500 cycles; run a bead control in parallel. Pre-stated kill threshold: drying k below 5e-3/s (less than 3.5x the beads), OR working capacity below 0.7 mmol/g in 10+10 min cycles (below about 2 kg/kg/day), OR cake pressure drop above 150 Pa at 10 mm/s, OR more than 5% mass loss or channelling over 500 cycles. Estimated cost $2-5k, 4-6 weeks.
ideas.computational_test: Couple the measured isotherms (Guzzo, Lopez-Marques) to an LDF cake model with water and CO2 co-transport and the latent-heat balance of the cake (evaporative cooling during drying, sorption heating during wetting). Find the cycle time at which air supply, water-vapour delivery or heat transfer becomes the limit, then feed the resulting productivity into a VMS-type energy and capital estimate.
ideas.conventional_core: Quaternary-ammonium anion-exchange resin in carbonate/bicarbonate form, moisture-swing regenerated (ASU/Lackner, IRA-900, A501).
ideas.graft: Binderless precoat filtration with finely ground ion-exchange resin, held by through-flow on a septum and renewed by back-pulse, as used in power-plant condensate polishing (water-treatment ion-exchange family).
ideas.why_different: It needs no new chemistry and no binder. It uses an existing commercial resin form and an existing industrial format to move the rate limit from intraparticle diffusion to air supply. It exploits the fact that inert mass is free in an isothermal swing, and it turns the poor field durability of resins into a powder-replacement operation.

ideas.title: Amino-acid-salt amines on a solid: carrying the oxidation resistance of potassium sarcosinate into a temperature-vacuum swing at 95 C or below
ideas.one_line: Liquid DAC work reports potassium sarcosinate losing no more than 2% after 500 h under O2, where MEA lost over 90%, but losing 21% after 700 h at 120 C. Supported amines are the reverse: thermally robust but oxidised at 55-90 C. Anchor alpha-amino-carboxylate sites on a solid regenerated at 95 C or below, so that each family is used only where it is strong.
ideas.mechanism: Solid-amine fade is dominated by radical autoxidation at C-H bonds alpha to nitrogen in PEI-type ethyleneamines, accelerated by 400 ppm CO2 below about 80 C. Amino-acid salts that bind CO2 by the same carbamate/bicarbonate chemistry are, in solution, at least 100 times more resistant to oxygen than MEA, but they degrade thermally above about 100-120 C. A solid temperature-vacuum swing that unloads at 92-95 C against 1 kPa CO2 (the verifier's window for a -70 kJ/mol site) never reaches the amino acid's thermal weak point, while the amine sites avoid the oxidation weak point. Design-level forms to compare: (a) potassium sarcosinate or glycinate dispersed on the same mesoporous silica used for PEI; (b) amino acids anchored through the carboxylate to Zr-oxo nodes (MOF-808-Lys type, already measured at 0.61 mmol/g dry and 1.2 mmol/g at 50% RH at 400 ppm); (c) carboxymethylated low-molecular-weight PEI (glycine-like secondary amines). Version (b) avoids the hygroscopic K+ carboxylate; (a) keeps the exact liquid motif. The question to test is whether the oxidation resistance transfers. It may partly reflect lower O2 solubility in concentrated salt solutions, or metal chelation by the amino acid, and neither effect carries over to a solid.
ideas.key_parameters: Site density about 3 mmol N/g (about 40 wt% of a potassium sarcosinate-type unit on silica). Binding needed: fill of at least 50% at 420 ppm and 25 C, i.e. dG of -19.2 kJ/mol or stronger, which means dH of -69 kJ/mol or stronger at dS -165 J/mol/K. Stoichiometry 0.5 CO2/N (carbamate, dry) to 1 CO2/N (bicarbonate, humid). Swing: adsorb at 25 C and 30-60% RH; desorb at 95 C (no higher) under 1 kPa CO2 by steam/vacuum. Water co-adsorption must stay at or below 4 mol H2O per mol CO2. Oxidative fade target at least 10x below PEI. Material cost: commodity amino acids plus silica, about $10-40/kg (not costed).
ideas.quantitative_claims: From g2_opus_ideas.py with TVSACycle (dS -165, 95 C, 1 kPa). (1) Liquid-phase first-order rates under O2 (Kiani 2024 as cited by ORNL; test temperature not stated in the citing text): MEA at least 4.6e-3/h versus sarcosine at most 4.0e-5/h, a ratio of at least 114x. Supported PEI at 60 C in dry 0.04% CO2 air degrades at 9.0e-3/h. (2) At 3 mmol N/g and dH -70 kJ/mol: carbamate mode gives wc 0.72 mol/kg and heat 6.9/8.9/10.9 GJ/t at 2/4/6 mol water per mol CO2; bicarbonate mode (humid) gives wc 1.45 mol/kg and heat 5.2/7.2/9.2 GJ/t. (3) Kill criterion: at dH -65 kJ/mol, fill is only 20% and wc 0.24-0.48 mol/kg, so heat rises to 8-17 GJ/t. (4) Each extra mol of water per mol CO2 from hygroscopic K+ carboxylate adds 1.0 GJ/t. (5) Sorbent cost from the verifier (wc 0.9 mol/kg): at 3.5e-3 %/cycle fade, $88/t at $20/kg and $177/t at $40/kg; with 10x slower fade, $9/t and $18/t; with 30x slower, $3/t and $6/t.
ideas.closest_known_work: MOF-808-Lys and MOF-808-TAPA (Chen, Yaghi et al., JACS 2024): amino acid on Zr nodes, 1 CO2 per amine when humid, no oxidative data. ORNL potassium sarcosinate liquid DAC contactors (2025) and the bis-iminoguanidine crystallisation route. Kiani et al. 2024 on amino-acid-salt oxidative and thermal degradation (as cited by ORNL OSTI 3002477; not opened). Epoxide-functionalised PEI with chelator (Min 2018). An aminopolymer aerogel patent claiming 7x oxidative stability from primary amines. Supported amino-acid ionic liquids for flue gas. No published solid amino-acid-salt DAC sorbent with oxidative ageing data was found in a quick search.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Prepare, at matched N loading (about 3 mmol N/g) on the same commercial mesoporous silica: (i) branched PEI 800; (ii) potassium sarcosinate; (iii) potassium glycinate. If MOF-808 can be made, add MOF-808-Lys. Measure 400 ppm CO2 uptake at 25 C, dry and at 50% RH, and the water isotherm at 50% RH. Age portions by the Li et al. JACS 2024 protocol for 18 h at 60 C and 70 C in 0.04% CO2 air, dry and at 50% RH, then re-measure capacity and N content. Pre-stated kill threshold: the amino-acid sorbent's fractional capacity loss at 70 C and 50% RH is more than one-fifth of PEI's (less than a 5x improvement), OR fresh capacity is below 0.6 mmol/g at 400 ppm, 50% RH and 25 C, OR water uptake exceeds 4 mol per mol CO2. Estimated cost $2-4k (thermogravimetric analysis plus elemental analysis), 3-4 weeks.
ideas.computational_test: Compute, with DFT or a cheaper semi-empirical method, the alpha C-H bond dissociation energies and peroxyl-radical H-abstraction barriers for sarcosinate, glycinate (free and with the carboxylate bound to Zr) and PEI ethyleneamine segments. Rank the barrier differences; trends are more reliable than absolute DFT binding energies, which carry errors of 10-20 kJ/mol. Separately, check carbamate and bicarbonate formation free energies against the verifier's 420 ppm fill window.
ideas.conventional_core: Supported-amine temperature-vacuum swing (PEI on mesoporous silica, regenerated at about 95 C under steam or vacuum).
ideas.graft: The oxidation-resistant alpha-amino-carboxylate (amino-acid-salt) CO2 site measured in liquid DAC solvents (potassium sarcosinate/glycinate), anchored on a solid as a salt or through the carboxylate to Zr-oxo nodes (MOF-808 family).
ideas.why_different: Rather than protecting PEI with additives, steric bulk or oxygen-free processing, it swaps in a site class whose measured weakness (thermal, above 100-120 C) lies outside the solid swing's window, and whose strength (oxygen resistance) covers the solid's weakness. The transfer itself is the untested claim, and one inexpensive ageing run settles it.

ideas.title: Soda-lime shuttle: a KOH film on passive Ca(OH)2 trays to carbonate in arid air
ideas.one_line: Passive lime trays only carbonate fast above about 50-80% RH. Borrow soda-lime chemistry from anaesthesia and rebreather absorbents: a few wt% KOH keeps a liquid film on the lime that captures CO2 quickly and is continuously regenerated by causticisation, so dry sunny sites can run lime DAC without humidification.
ideas.mechanism: Ca(OH)2 carbonation proceeds through a nanometre water film. It is extremely slow below 50% RH and gives under 5% conversion in dry air (Criado and Abanades 2022), which ties Heirloom-type plants to humid sites. Humidifying 20%-RH air to 80% would take about 37 t of water per t CO2. Soda lime (Ca(OH)2 with a few percent NaOH, measured for decades as an anaesthesia and rebreather CO2 absorbent) works by a shuttle: hydroxide in a liquid film absorbs CO2 to carbonate, and the carbonate reacts with solid Ca(OH)2 to give CaCO3 and regenerate the hydroxide. KOH is the better promoter for arid air because KOH stays deliquescent down to about 8% RH (general knowledge), while Na2CO3 does not. The captured carbon ends up as CaCO3 and goes to the usual electric kiln. Most potassium stays with the CaO and re-forms KOH on slaking. Kim et al. 2025 showed that concentrated KOH films capture air CO2 passively at high flux but crystallise K2CO3, which needs electrochemical regeneration; here the lime is the carbonate sink instead.
ideas.key_parameters: Sorbent: high-surface-area Ca(OH)2 (39 m2/g grade) with 2-4 wt% KOH, in 2-4 mm layers. Adsorption at ambient temperature and 15-40% RH, 420 ppm, 1-3 day cycles. Capture thermodynamics are strongly over-binding: calcination reaction heat 178 kJ/mol (4.05 GJ/t) at about 900 C, unchanged by the additive. Kiln duty 5.8-7.1 GJ/t (50% to no sensible-heat recovery, OptiLex map). Lime about $0.15/kg; KOH about $1/kg; K loss per calcination unknown (5-20% assumed). Product: pure CO2 from the electric kiln.
ideas.quantitative_claims: From g2_opus_ideas.py. (1) Ideal-solution causticisation equilibrium, K = Ksp(Ca(OH)2)/Ksp(CaCO3) = 1,471 M, leaves only 0.07 M carbonate at 10 M OH- and 0.13 M at 14 M OH-. The shuttle is therefore thermodynamically allowed even in the concentrated films expected at 15-40% RH. Activity coefficients and the kinetics of Ca(OH)2 dissolution in strong KOH are the unknowns. (2) If the film removes the humidity limit, flux becomes CO2-supply-limited: about 80-145 kg/m2/yr at 1-3 day cycles by a Fick front model (the OptiLex map's model gives 119 at 3 days; measured humid beds 12-117). (3) KOH make-up at 2-4 wt% of Ca(OH)2 (40-79 kg per t CO2 cycled) and 5-20% loss per calcination costs $2-16/t. Film water carried to the kiln adds 0.15-0.29 GJ/t. (4) No energy gain: calcination remains 4.05 GJ/t of reaction heat and 5.8-7.1 GJ/t total, so this idea is siting and kinetics only. (5) The alternative, humidifying 20%-RH air to 80%, costs about 37 t water per t CO2.
ideas.closest_known_work: Soda lime and soda-lime-type absorbents (NaOH-promoted Ca(OH)2) in anaesthesia and rebreathers. Kim et al., Nature Chem. Eng. 2025: passive DAC by evaporative KOH crystallisation on a wicking substrate, with flux over 6x conventional contactors and electrochemical regeneration. Criado and Abanades, IECR 2022, and Criado et al. 2026: Ca(OH)2 carbonation versus RH. Dostie, Rausis and Power 2024-25: a humidity swing reaching over 85% conversion. Heirloom trays (Ca(OH)2, about 3-day cycles). No DAC study of KOH-promoted lime trays in arid air was found in a quick search; Heirloom patents were not checked.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Spread 2-4 mm layers of high-surface Ca(OH)2 with 0, 1, 2 and 4 wt% KOH, plus a 4 wt% NaOH control, in a fan-ventilated chamber at 25 C and 420 ppm, at 20%, 35% and 50% RH, for 3 and 7 days. Measure conversion by thermogravimetric analysis and the location of carbonate (CaCO3 versus K2CO3) by XRD. Then put the best sample through 5 cycles of calcination at 900 C and steam slaking, tracking K retention by ICP and CaO reactivity. Pre-stated kill threshold: at 35% RH the 4 wt% KOH layer reaches less than 40% conversion in 3 days or less than 3x the undoped control, OR K2CO3 crystals hold more than 30% of the captured CO2, OR K loss exceeds 20% per calcination, OR CaO re-carbonation capacity falls more than 10% per cycle relative to undoped lime. Estimated cost about $2k, 4-6 weeks.
ideas.computational_test: A Pitzer-model calculation of causticisation equilibrium and film water activity for KOH-K2CO3-Ca(OH)2-H2O at 15-50% RH and 10-40 C, to map where the film stays liquid and carbonate stays below K2CO3 saturation. Then couple this to the existing Fick front model to predict conversion versus time and RH, and price tray area and K make-up per tonne against real desert climate records.
ideas.conventional_core: Passive Ca(OH)2 carbonation on trays with electric-kiln calcination (lime looping, Heirloom type).
ideas.graft: The soda-lime hydroxide shuttle (alkali hydroxide film catalysing Ca(OH)2 carbonation), measured in anaesthesia and rebreather CO2 absorbents and related to the KOH evaporative crystalliser.
ideas.why_different: It targets the humidity window, the one lime bottleneck that the cheap-sorbent economics cannot absorb, without humidification or electrochemistry. The verifier shows it leaves the 900 C energy bill unchanged, so its value is siting (dry, sunny, cheap-power land) and tray speed, not efficiency.

ideas.title: Moisture-swing resin as a passive 50-100x pre-concentrator for an O2-tolerant MnO2 electro-swing cell
ideas.one_line: Air-breathing electrochemical DAC cells are capped near 2-8 mA/cm2 by gas-film CO2 supply at 420 ppm. A moisture-swing resin can lift CO2 to 2-4 kPa in a closed humid 1-atm loop with no heat. That lets the MnO2 surface-mineralisation cell work in its measured 4% CO2 regime (about 1.7 GJ/t at 50 mA/cm2) instead of its air regime (3.9-4.1 GJ/t at 1 mA/cm2).
ideas.mechanism: Stage 1: carbonate-form quaternary-ammonium resin (IRA-900/A501, or the precoat of the powdered-resin idea) loads CO2 from dry ambient air. It is then moved, or switched by valves, into a closed loop of humid air at 1 atm, where wetting raises its CO2 equilibrium about 100-fold (Wang/Lackner; up to 6 kPa needed to saturate wet resin, Guzzo et al.), so the loop climbs to about 2-4% CO2 with no heat and no vacuum vessel. Stage 2: the loop gas passes a MnO2 gas-diffusion cell. Reduced Mn-O- sites bind CO2 as surface bicarbonate/carbonate, and re-oxidation releases pure CO2. The Sargent/Farha device was measured as insensitive to O2 and humidity in air and gave about 1.7 GJ/t, about 300 t CO2 per t sorbent per year and 70% single-pass removal at 4% CO2 and 50 mA/cm2. Because the loop carries air, a CO2-selective second stage is needed; vacuum alone cannot separate CO2 from air at 1 atm. MnO2 suits this because O2 is only about 5x CO2 in the loop rather than 500x in ambient air, and it is already proven at 4%.
ideas.key_parameters: Stage 1: resin swing about 0.5-1.2 mmol/g, loading 0.8-1.9 mmol/g dry at 400 ppm and 15-20% RH and releasing to at most 0.3-0.4 mmol/g wet at 2-4 kPa; water 17-24 mol per mol CO2 in vapour mode, latent heat from ambient air; resin $10-20/kg. Loop: 1 atm humid air with 2-4% CO2, about 50% stripped per pass, 300 Pa. Stage 2: MnO2 redox potential about 0.7 V vs RHE, roughly one electron per CO2 in principle; measured coulombic efficiency 22-33% in air; 50 mA/cm2 and 1.7 GJ/t measured at 4% CO2 (N2-balanced); cell cost assumed $300-1,000/m2; electrode and counter-electrode life about 1,000 h so far (counter electrode replaced at about 210 h).
ideas.quantitative_claims: From g2_opus_ideas.py, using FARADAY and fan_work from the verifiers. (1) The gas-film CO2 supply cap at 420 ppm is 1.7-8.3 mA/cm2 at one electron per CO2 for k_g of 0.01-0.05 m/s; at 3 kPa it is 117-584 mA/cm2. (2) Cell areal productivity (half duty) is 0.018 t/m2/yr at 1 mA/cm2 and coulombic efficiency 0.25 (measured MnO2 in air: 0.0084), versus 1.08-2.88 t/m2/yr at 50 mA/cm2 and efficiency 0.30-0.80. The cell capital charge (14%/yr) falls from $2,334-7,780/t to $15-130/t at $300-1,000/m2. (3) Electricity: 1.7 GJ/t cell (measured at 4%) + 0.02 GJ/t loop blower + 0.29 GJ/t resin-bed fan at 100 Pa = 2.0 GJ/t (559 kWh/t, 23% second-law, $28/t at $50/MWh). At 2.5 GJ/t cell energy the total is 2.8 GJ/t (17%). This is comparable to the modelled 2.5 GJ/t for vacuum moisture swing and below the measured 3.9-4.1 GJ/t (plus 1-2 GJ/t vacuum and compression) for the MnO2 cell fed with air. (4) Stage 1 releases 0.5-1.2 mmol/g into a 2-4 kPa loop, a 50-100x enrichment over 42.6 Pa.
ideas.closest_known_work: Liu, Sargent et al., Nature Energy 2026 (doi 10.1038/s41560-026-01989-9): MnO2 cell in air (3.9-4.1 GJ/t, 1 mA/cm2, over 1,000 h) and at 4% CO2 (about 1.7 GJ/t at 50 mA/cm2). Sinyangwe, Wade et al. 2026: vacuum moisture swing, simulated. ASU outdoor moisture-swing pilot (Flory 2025). Avnos hybrid moisture-swing DAC (company claims only). Within OptiLex, pass 1 proposed resin capture plus MnO2 proton-sponge release from a liquid bicarbonate eluate; this idea differs by using a gas-phase 1-atm loop and the gas-diffusion surface-mineralisation cell at its measured 4% operating point.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Stage 1 alone, about $2k. Load carbonate-form IRA-900 (10 g, or the powder precoat) with 400 ppm air at 20% RH. Then close it into a 1-atm recirculating air loop at 90-95% RH with an NDIR sensor, and measure the CO2 plateau, release rate and amount released while the loop is held at 2, 3 and 4 kPa by a bleed. Stage 2, about $5-10k at a group already running MnO2 gas-diffusion cells: run at 2-3% CO2 in humid air with 21% O2. Pre-stated kill threshold: loop plateau below 1.5 kPa, OR less than 0.4 mmol/g released against 1.5 kPa back-pressure; OR the MnO2 cell at 2-3% CO2 in humid air cannot sustain at least 20 mA/cm2 with at least 50% single-pass removal at 2.5 GJ/t or less (cell electricity) over 100 h.
ideas.computational_test: Loop mass balance using the Guzzo/Lopez-Marques co-sorption isotherms (CO2 loading versus pCO2, RH and T) to find the optimum loop CO2 level, trading resin working capacity against cell current density and energy. Then a Faraday-plus-capital model (already scripted) sweeping coulombic efficiency, current density, $/m2 and electrode life against vacuum moisture swing with vacuum vessels.
ideas.conventional_core: O2-tolerant MnO2 electro-swing (surface-mineralisation) cell for CO2 capture and release.
ideas.graft: Passive moisture-swing CO2 enrichment by quaternary-ammonium resins (dry loading, wet release into a closed humid loop), measured in the moisture-swing family.
ideas.why_different: It removes the electrochemical family's binding constraint, areal productivity set by CO2 supply at 420 ppm, by moving the cell to a measured flue-gas-like operating point. It also removes the moisture-swing family's need for vacuum-rated resin vessels. Each family does only the job it has measured data for.

ideas.title: In-place reductive repair of oxidised amine sorbents (imine back to amine), borrowed from post-synthetic reduction of imine-linked COFs
ideas.one_line: Oxidised PEI sorbents carry mostly imine and carbonyl products, and the DOE field pilot reported oxidation with mechanically intact beds. If a large share of the lost sites are imines still attached to the polymer, a periodic mild hydride reduction (the measured route from imine-linked to amine-linked COFs) could restore them in place and extend sorbent life.
ideas.mechanism: Autoxidation of supported PEI goes through hydroperoxides to imines, carbonyls and amides, with some C-N scission and volatile loss. Imine C=N sites are no longer basic but keep their nitrogen on the polymer. The COF family routinely converts imine linkages to amine linkages by post-synthetic borohydride reduction, retaining framework and porosity, which shows the reaction is compatible with porous solids. Applied to a faded DAC laminate taken off-line every few thousand cycles, mild reduction would turn imines back into secondary amines and aldehydes into alcohols. Amides and lost fragments stay lost. The idea is worthwhile only if the reducible fraction of the damage is large, and the measurement also separates conversion damage (repairable) from loss damage, which the OptiLex map lists as open. Hazard note: the reductant is a standard laboratory hydride used at design level; no procedure is given here.
ideas.key_parameters: Core: PEI/silica laminate, dH about -70 kJ/mol, dS about -165 J/mol/K, wc 1.04 mol/kg at 100 C and 1 kPa; fade 2.2e-3 to 3.5e-3 %/cycle. Repair: every 2,000-3,000 cycles, off-line wet treatment with a mild hydride reductant, then wash and dry; reagent 9-35 g per kg sorbent if 10% of N must be restored (0.25-1 mol hydride per C=N); repair cost assumed $1.5-4 per kg sorbent per treatment. Unknown: the reducible share r of the damage.
ideas.quantitative_claims: From g2_opus_ideas.py, using the verifier's sorbent cost ($20/kg, wc 1.04). (1) Fade 3.5e-3 %/cycle with r = 50%, repaired every 2,000 cycles at $1.5/kg: life 5,714 to 11,429 cycles; sorbent $76/t to $38/t plus $16/t repair, a net saving of $22/t. (2) With r = 30%, the net saving is $7/t. (3) At 2.2e-3 %/cycle with r = 50% every 3,000 cycles, net saving $13/t. (4) At $4/kg per repair the idea loses money (-$5/t). So it needs r of at least about 30-40% and repairs at $1.5/kg or less to be worth deploying. Its diagnostic value (repairable versus lost damage) holds either way.
ideas.closest_known_work: Post-synthetic NaBH4 reduction of imine-linked COFs to amine-linked COFs with retained porosity (e.g. Chem. Commun. 2023, D3CC00851G; Chem. Sci. 2025, d5sc02492g). Studies of oxidised PEI on alumina reporting predominantly imine and carbonyl products (Jones group, AIChE 2020; Li et al. JACS 2024). DOE pilot DE-FE0031952 autopsy: oxidation with intact mechanics. MEA reclaiming in liquid amine plants. Within OptiLex, pass 1 proposed strip-and-reload refurbishment and dynamic-covalent anchors; this idea repairs the sites in place rather than replacing the amine. No published reduction-based repair of a DAC sorbent was found in a quick search.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Age 40 wt% PEI/silica for 18 h at 70 C in 0.04% CO2 air to about 20-40% capacity loss, recording the FTIR imine band (about 1,660-1,670 cm-1) and carbonyl bands. Split the aged sample: one part gets solvent only, another gets a mild hydride reduction at room temperature, followed by a wash and dry. Re-measure 400 ppm CO2 capacity (25 C, 50% RH), FTIR and N content. Re-age both once more to check whether the repaired material fades faster. Pre-stated kill threshold: repair recovers less than 25% of the lost capacity, OR the repaired sample's second fade rate is more than 1.5x that of fresh sorbent, OR residual boron or sodium exceeds 0.5 wt% after a standard wash. Estimated cost about $1-2k, 2-3 weeks.
ideas.computational_test: Kinetic bookkeeping model: split the measured fade into imine, amide/carbonyl and volatile fractions using FTIR/NMR quantification, and simulate repeated repair over 20,000 cycles to find the optimal repair interval against reagent and handling cost with the verifier's sorbent-cost function. A DFT check of whether reduced imines regenerate secondary amines with carbamate binding inside the -70 kJ/mol window.
ideas.conventional_core: Supported PEI/silica laminate in a steam/vacuum temperature swing.
ideas.graft: Post-synthetic imine-to-amine linkage reduction measured in the COF family (borohydride reduction of imine-linked frameworks).
ideas.why_different: Earlier durability ideas either prevent oxidation (antioxidants, oxygen-free cool-down, steric protection) or replace the amine (strip and reload). This one repairs the converted sites chemically in place. It is the only idea here whose main deliverable is diagnostic, splitting oxidative damage into repairable and permanent fractions; deployment value is a modest $7-22/t.

ideas.title: Nanoceria as a catalytic, non-consumable HO2*/H2O2 scavenger inside supported PEI
ideas.one_line: Mix 1-3 wt% CeO2 particles a few nm across into PEI on alumina or silica. The Ce3+/Ce4+ couple should keep removing HO2* and H2O2, the species modelled as carrying PEI autoxidation, the way ceria protects fuel-cell membranes, and unlike organic antioxidants it should not be used up.
ideas.mechanism: PEI fades at DAC conditions by radical autoxidation. A molecular-modelling study (Nanomaterials 2025, doi 10.3390/nano15040313; simulation, low weight) names two main propagation routes: HO2* acting as the chain carrier, and alpha-aminoalkyl radicals reacting with H2O2, put at about 50% of propagation. Amide and imine units make up about 90% of fully oxidised PEI in that study. CeO2 surfaces switch between Ce3+ and Ce4+. This lets them dismutate superoxide/HO2* and decompose H2O2 to O2 + H2O without releasing free radicals (the SOD- and catalase-like activity of nanoceria). In PEM fuel cells ceria additives cut fluoride emission (membrane chain scission) by about 10x in Fenton tests (UCF work, via search). Ceria is inorganic, involatile, insoluble in steam and basic media, and sits in the polymer for the sorbent's whole life. Organic traps, by contrast, are consumed: under dry 0.04% CO2-air at 70 C, 2 mol% BDDPA held loss near 0% for 4.5 h but 30% by 18 h (Guta et al., Energy Fuels 2025, PMC12703673). Three risks could make ceria harmful. (1) Ce4+/Ce3+ could cycle alkyl hydroperoxides into RO*/ROO*, as Co and Mn paint driers do. (2) Ceria is reported in synthesis work as a catalyst for turning amines plus CO2 into ureas (not re-verified here). (3) Acidic Ce sites could tie up some amine. The cheap test below checks all three.
ideas.key_parameters: CO2 binding is unchanged. Verifier reference: dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, q_max 2.0 mol/kg (measured PEI heats are 66-80 kJ/mol). Cycle: adsorb at 25 C and 42 Pa CO2, desorb at 100 C and 1 kPa CO2, 2 mol H2O per mol CO2, 30-min cycles. With 3 wt% CeO2 of 3-5 nm (cp about 460 J/kg/K): working capacity 1.011 mol/kg (vs 1.042), heat 6.07 GJ/t (vs 6.04), work-equivalent 1.88 GJ/t, ideal second-law efficiency 24.7%. Lifetime target: cut fade from about 5e-3 to at most 1.1e-3 %/cycle, i.e. 20% loss at 20,000 cycles. Material cost: $20/kg sorbent plus about $0.6/kg of ceria (nano-CeO2 assumed at $20/kg; bulk CeO2 costs a few $/kg).
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) Verifier: 1/3/5 wt% CeO2 gives working capacity 1.032/1.011/0.990 mol/kg and heat 6.05/6.07/6.08 GJ/t (reference 1.042 mol/kg, 6.04 GJ/t). (2) Stoichiometric scavenging alone would run out fast. A 45 wt% PEI sorbent has 10.45 mol N/kg; at fade 2.2e-3 to 5e-3 %/cycle it loses 230-522 umol N/kg per cycle. Dividing by chain lengths of 1-5 gives 46-522 umol of radicals per kg per cycle to intercept. Surface Ce on 3 wt% ceria (3-10 nm particles) is 14-46 mmol/kg, so a one-shot charge lasts 27-1,009 cycles. 20,000 cycles need 20-750 turnovers per surface Ce, so the ceria must work catalytically. (3) Levelized model built on the verifier (capital $274/t with 60% scaling with productivity, $20/kg sorbent, replacement interval optimised, base $417/t). If ceria has no effect it adds $10/t (capacity dilution). If it divides fade by 2/5/10 it saves $24/$52/$65 per t. For a $50/kg sorbent the savings are $49/$97/$119 per t. (4) Even a perfect stop to fade only takes the base from $417/t to $317/t; capital stays dominant.
ideas.closest_known_work: Ceria and Ce3+ radical scavengers in PEM fuel-cell membranes (Gore/3M-type practice; UCF studies show about 10x lower fluoride emission). Kuwahara, Jones et al. 2012 (Chem. Eur. J., doi 10.1002/chem.201203144) put Ce, Zr, Ti or Al into the SBA-15 framework under PEI and found acid-base gains in capacity and regenerability, but tested in Ar with no O2. Guta et al. 2025 tested organic radical traps (BDDPA best, but depleted or overwhelmed). Min et al. 2018 used chelators plus epoxybutane. Searches of Europe PMC and the web (Oct 2026) found no use of ceria as an oxidation scavenger in amine CO2 sorbents; the search was limited.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Follow the Li 2024 / Guta 2025 protocol on 45 wt% branched PEI-800 on gamma-Al2O3, with 0, 1 and 3 wt% ceria dispersion (3-5 nm and 20 nm). Age the samples (TGA, mg scale) under four conditions: (a) 4.5 h at 120 C in dry CO2-free air; (b) 18 h at 70 C in dry 0.04% CO2-air; (c) 18 h at 70 C in the same gas at about 43% RH; (d) 30 TSA cycles (adsorb at 30 C in humid 400 ppm air, desorb at 100 C in N2, readmit air at 70 C). Read capacity at 30 C and 400 ppm. Add a 4-ppm-Cu-doped arm and a urea check: 24 h at 110 C in dry CO2, then FTIR at about 1650-1700 cm-1. Pre-stated go: in (b), (c) and (d) the ceria sample loses no more than half of the control's capacity loss; fresh capacity penalty at most 5%; no extra urea band. Kill: loss at least equal to the control in any O2 condition (pro-oxidant), or more urea than the control. Cost: about $3-5k (TGA time, commercial nanoceria, about 2 months).
ideas.computational_test: Solve the PEI autoxidation rate equations (initiation, HO2* and ROO* propagation with H2O2 cross-reactions as in the Nanomaterials 2025 scheme, termination) with an added heterogeneous first-order sink for HO2* and H2O2 that scales with ceria surface area. Find the surface rate constant that cuts the chain rate 5x and compare it with published nanoceria SOD- and catalase-mimetic rate constants. If the required constant is more than 10x the measured ones, deprioritise. The levelized and verifier numbers above are in climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/p2_durability.py (output: p2_durability_output.txt).
ideas.conventional_core: PEI or TEPA impregnated in porous alumina or silica, used in steam-assisted temperature-vacuum swing (the commercial solid-amine baseline).
ideas.graft: The ceria radical-scavenger additive from PEM fuel-cell membrane durability (regenerative Ce3+/Ce4+ quenching of HO*/HO2* and decomposition of H2O2).
ideas.why_different: Every amine-sorbent stabiliser tested so far is organic and consumable (diarylamines, HALS, nitroxides, sulfur additives) or a chelator. Ceria is an inorganic catalytic scavenger aimed at the specific chain carriers (HO2*, H2O2) that recent modelling assigns to PEI. It does not need topping up, cannot evaporate or leach in steam, and costs under 5% capacity.

ideas.title: In-place reductive reclaiming: reduce oxidation-born imines back to amines with borohydride (plus a base wash)
ideas.one_line: Treat oxidised amine sorbent in place with a short alkaline borohydride wash every few thousand cycles. The wash turns C=N imines and aldehyde-amine condensates back into CO2-binding amines, and the base frees amines held as salts of acidic oxidation products, so capacity is restored rather than replaced.
ideas.mechanism: In-situ IR of PEI/Al2O3 oxidised in 0.04% CO2-air shows two bands: imine C=N at 1648 cm-1 and carbonyl C=O at 1671 cm-1 (Guta et al., ACS AMI 2023, PMC10571043). C-N cleavage also gives new primary amines and aminoacetaldehyde-type fragments, which can recondense with amines into imines. Modelling puts amide plus imine units at about 90% of fully oxidised PEI (simulation). Imines (and aldehydes plus neighbouring amines, by reductive amination) are reduced by BH4- to secondary amines, which bind CO2 again. Amides and ureas are not reduced, so they set the irreversible fraction. A dilute base step frees amine sites tied up as ammonium formate, oxalate or glycolate. That is the known amine-reclaiming principle, already patented for SO2-derived heat-stable salts on solid beds. Liquid water redistributes or leaches impregnated PEI, so the wash suits crosslinked or tethered amines: benzylamine resins such as Lewatit VP OC 1065, aminosilane-grafted oxides, epoxide-crosslinked PEI, and COF-tethered PEI. Impregnated PEI would need a non-solvent medium, which is untested. Borohydride gives off H2 on contact with water and acid. It is handled at industrial scale in pulp bleaching; this is a design-level note only.
ideas.key_parameters: Binding is unchanged for restored sites. Reference dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K; secondary amines bind somewhat more weakly than primary ones. Base cycle: working capacity 1.04 mol/kg, 100 C and 1 kPa desorption, 30-min cycles, base fade 5e-3 %/cycle. Repair every 2,000-5,000 cycles (42-104 days). Reagent: 0.1-0.25 mol NaBH4 per kg per repair (3-fold excess over 0.1-0.3 mol/kg of imine-type sites per 10% capacity loss), i.e. 3.8-9.5 g/kg, $0.11-0.28/kg at an assumed $30/kg. Repair cost including handling assumed $0.3-3/kg per event, with 1 day of downtime. The governing unknown is the reversible fraction r of the capacity loss.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) Levelized verifier-based model (base $417/t at $20/kg). For r = 0/0.25/0.50/0.75, at $1/kg per repair with 1 day down, cost changes by +$1/-$3/-$14/-$32 per t (best repair interval 3,000-8,000 cycles). At r = 0.5: -$19/t at $0.3/kg per repair, -$5/t at $3/kg. For a $50/kg sorbent at r = 0.5: -$37/t. (2) Drying 1 kg of water per kg sorbent after each wash costs only 0.011-0.018 GJ/t CO2 for repairs every 5,000-3,000 cycles. (3) The idea pays only if at least about 40% of the lost capacity is reversible. Below r = 0.25 the gain is under $5/t, so it should be dropped.
ideas.closest_known_work: US 9,101,912 (Alstom, now GE Vernova; priority 2012): dilute NaOH/KOH washing of solid amine beds to break SO2-derived heat-stable salts, with no recovery figures and no oxidation repair. Liquid-amine reclaiming practice, plus US 11,607,642 (seen as a search snippet only), which reductively aminates imine-dimer degradation products in liquid absorbents. An earlier scratch calculation in this run (durability_ideas.py) priced stripping the amine and reloading new amine. No published reductive repair of oxidised solid DAC sorbents was found (limited search).
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Age two substrates to 30-40% capacity loss: 45 wt% PEI-800/gamma-Al2O3, and Lewatit VP OC 1065 (insoluble benzylamine resin), both for 24 h at 80 C in 21% O2 air with 0.04% CO2. Add a PEI sample aged 2 months at 40 C under N2, which tests the unexplained non-oxidative loss. Split each into four arms: (i) solvent wash only (controls for amine redistribution and leaching; measure N by CHN); (ii) dilute NaOH or Na2CO3 only; (iii) alkaline NaBH4 only; (iv) base then NaBH4. Dry, then measure 400 ppm CO2 capacity at 30 C (dry and 50% RH), the FTIR 1648/1671 cm-1 band areas, and CHN. Pre-stated go: arm (iv) recovers at least 30% of the lost capacity beyond arm (i), and the 1648 cm-1 band falls by at least 50%. Kill: under 10% recovery beyond the wash control. Cost: about $1-2k, a few weeks.
ideas.computational_test: Build a site mass balance. Calibrate the IR 1648 cm-1 (imine) and 1671 cm-1 (amide/carbonyl) absorptivities on model compounds (an N-alkyl aldimine and an N-alkylacetamide), convert band areas of aged sorbents into site counts, and predict recoverable capacity as about 0.5 CO2 per restored N (carbamate) or 1 per N (humid bicarbonate). Then run the repair-economics model (repair_direct in p2_durability.py) with the measured r. The test passes if predicted and measured recovery agree within a factor of 1.5.
ideas.conventional_core: A crosslinked or tethered amine sorbent (benzylamine resin, aminosilane-grafted oxide, or epoxide-crosslinked or COF-tethered PEI) used in steam-assisted TVSA.
ideas.graft: Amine reclaiming plus borohydride or reductive-amination chemistry from amine manufacture and liquid-amine plants, used to undo oxidation in place rather than to clean a liquid solvent.
ideas.why_different: Durability work so far either slows damage or replaces the sorbent, either whole or as fresh amine on the old support. This idea treats part of the damage as chemically reversible and restores sites in place for well under $1/kg per event. It also gives the first measured split between reversible damage (imine, salt) and irreversible damage (amide, urea, scission), which no study has reported.

ideas.title: Site-specific isotope reinforcement: alpha-deuterated amines for expensive tethered-amine frameworks
ideas.one_line: Swap the alpha C-H bonds of the amine for C-D by Ru-catalysed exchange in D2O. Hydrogen abstraction, the propagation step of autoxidation, slows by the kinetic isotope effect, while CO2 binding stays the same. This pays only where the scaffold, not the amine, sets the sorbent price.
ideas.mechanism: PEI oxidation propagates by abstraction of alpha-amino C-H hydrogens by HO2* and ROO* (the 2025 modelling study; Li et al. JACS 2024). In autoxidation the rate scales with kp. Making those bonds C-D lowers kp by the primary KIE. The semiclassical zero-point-energy bound computed here is 4.4-5.3 at 60-100 C; tunnelling can push it higher, and lipid 'isotope reinforcement' measured KIE 12.8 +/- 0.6 for propagation (11,11-D2-linoleate, Free Radic Biol Med 2012). Deuterated OLED hosts showed up to 8x longer T90 lifetimes (ACS AMI 2023). The swap leaves geometry, basicity and CO2 binding unchanged; the secondary equilibrium isotope effect is well under 1 kJ/mol. That contrasts with the Long-group fix (fully substituted alpha-carbons in tmen), which costs loading and cooperativity. Heterogeneous Ru/C catalyses alpha-selective H/D exchange of primary and secondary alkylamines in D2O. In PEI every CH2 is alpha to a nitrogen, so all C-H positions are reachable. If metal-catalysed initiation or CO2-catalysed C-N cleavage limits the rate instead of propagation, the benefit shrinks. The test is built to detect that.
ideas.key_parameters: Binding is unchanged (reference dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, q_max 2 mol/kg, or about 2.5 mol/kg for a COF-type scaffold). Full alpha-deuteration needs at least 0.93 kg D2O per kg PEI (4 C-H per C2H5N unit; 8.5 wt% D in the product), 1.2-2x that in practice. Price premium = amine mass fraction x D2O use x D2O price: $134/kg sorbent (40% amine, $300/kg D2O, 1.2x use) up to $744/kg ($1,000/kg, 2x). Target effective KIE at least 3 at 60-100 C. Lifetime: fade 5e-3 %/cycle divided by the effective KIE. Swing: 25 C/42 Pa to 100 C/1 kPa, 30-min cycles.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) Semiclassical KIE (stretch ZPE 4.61 kJ/mol): 6.4 at 25 C, 5.3 at 60 C, 5.0 at 70 C, 4.4 at 100 C. (2) Linear mixing: deuterating a fraction x of sites gives kp_eff/kp_H = (1-x) + x/KIE, so 20% deuteration gives only a 13-18% rate cut, unless the non-linear protection seen with 20% D-PUFA in yeast carries over. (3) Levelized model, 98% deuteration, D2O at $300/kg with 1.2x use. PEI/silica at $20/kg: +$80/t at KIE 3, +$22/t at KIE 6, -$16/t at KIE 12.8, so not worth it for commodity sorbents. A COF/MOF-tethered amine at $100/kg (30% amine, working capacity 1.30): -$45/t (KIE 3), -$100/t (KIE 6), -$136/t (KIE 12.8). At $200/kg: -$123/-$197/-$244 per t. At $600/kg D2O the $100/kg case breaks even near KIE 3.5. (4) Supply limit: with a 20,000-cycle life and 40% amine, D2O demand is 0.61 kt/yr per Mt CO2/yr and 61 kt/yr per 100 Mt/yr. The reported heavy-water market of about $57M/yr (2024) implies only about 100-200 t/yr at $300-600/kg, so above about 0.3 Mt/yr this needs new deuterium production.
ideas.closest_known_work: Deuterated PUFAs (Hill, Shchepinov et al. 2012, doi 10.1016/j.freeradbiomed.2012.06.004; propagation KIE 12.8); deuterated OLED materials (ACS AMI 2023, doi 10.1021/acsami.2c22882; up to 8x T90). Xiong/Long JACS 2025: tmen with fully substituted alpha-carbons kept about 98% of amine after 10 days in O2 at 100 C but reached lower loading. Ru/C alpha-H/D exchange of amines (Sajiki and others). No deuterated CO2 sorbent was found in web or Europe PMC searches.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Deuterate TEPA or PEI-800 with Ru/C in D2O; target at least 90% alpha-D by 1H/2H NMR. Run a protio control through the identical Ru/C treatment in H2O and filter both; confirm Ru below 1 ppm by ICP. Impregnate both on gamma-Al2O3 (45 wt%). Age side by side: 18 h at 60 and 70 C in dry 0.04% CO2-air, 18 h at 70 C at 43% RH, and 4.5 h at 120 C in CO2-free air. Measure 400 ppm capacity at 30 C. Define KIE_eff = ln(retention_H)/ln(retention_D). Pre-stated go: KIE_eff of at least 3 at 70 C (humid and dry) with fresh capacity within 3%. Kill: KIE_eff of 1.5 or less, which would also show that propagation is not rate-limiting, a useful mechanistic result either way. Cost: about $3k (200 g D2O, Ru/C, NMR, TGA).
ideas.computational_test: DFT transition states (e.g. a range-separated hybrid with dispersion) for HO2* abstraction of the alpha-H from N,N'-dimethylethylenediamine and from its alpha-amino hydroperoxide, with Eckart tunnelling, give a predicted KIE at 60-100 C. Deprioritise if below 2.5. Then put the predicted KIE into the levelized model (section 3 of p2_durability.py) for each scaffold price.
ideas.conventional_core: Amine chemisorbent: PEI or TEPA on oxide, or PEI tethered in a COF/MOF (COF-999/COF-1000 class), used in TVSA.
ideas.graft: Site-specific isotope reinforcement from lipid-peroxidation drug design (D-PUFAs) and deuterated OLED hosts.
ideas.why_different: Every other oxidation-resistant amine design changes the chemistry: alkyl substitution, epoxide hydroxyls, or spacer length. Each of those also shifts binding enthalpy or density, and the verifier shows that weakening binding by 5 kJ/mol costs about $570/t. Deuteration leaves binding intact and targets only the rate-limiting H transfer. The cost analysis turns it into a precise niche: worth it for $100-200/kg framework sorbents, not for $20/kg PEI/silica, and capped by deuterium supply.

ideas.title: Polymer-bound Cu deactivator (jet-fuel DMD-type salicylaldimine, or tolyltriazole) sized for metal pick-up in service
ideas.one_line: React about 0.5 mol% of the PEI amines with salicylaldehyde to give tethered salicylaldimine ligands, a polymer-bound copy of the jet-fuel metal deactivator DMD. They lock incoming Cu (and Fe) from dust and boiler steam into redox-inert chelates for the sorbent's whole life, at a 0.7% capacity cost.
ideas.mechanism: About 4 ppm Cu raised PEI/SBA-15 deactivation from 28% to 37% capacity loss (retention 72% to 63%), and 1000:1 PEI:metal (about 40 ppm) to 50-75% loss, after 4.5 h at 120 C in dry air (Kuspangaliyeva, Lively, Jones, ES&T 2026, PMC13235560). That paper notes that chelators added at synthesis may fail against metals arriving continuously from steam (Isenberg and Chuang found Cu, Fe and Zn in boiler steam) and from dust. In jet fuel, N,N'-disalicylidene-1,2-propanediamine (DMD) at mg/L levels stops dissolved Cu from catalysing hydroperoxide breakdown (standard fuel-spec practice; not re-verified here). Salicylaldehyde reacts with primary amines on PEI to form the same N,O-salicylaldimine donor set in the polymer. Cu(II) bis(salicylaldiminato) N2O2 chelates are square planar and redox-sluggish, whereas Cu-polyamine complexes are the active catalysts. Excess amine keeps the imine-forming equilibrium on the bound side even in steam. Tolyltriazole, the lubricant and corrosion-inhibitor Cu passivator, is a non-phenolic second candidate. Risks: phenols can speed amine oxidation (Guta review); the ligand might not out-compete PEI for Cu; and Fe from mineral dust is mostly insoluble, so Cu may matter more.
ideas.key_parameters: Binding is unchanged (reference dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K). Ligand: 0.5 mol% of N = 52 mmol/kg on a 45 wt% PEI sorbent (10.45 mol N/kg). That holds 26 mmol Cu/kg as CuL2, about 1,660 ppm Cu. Salicylaldehyde needed: 6.4 g/kg, about $0.03/kg at $5/kg. Working capacity 1.035 mol/kg (vs 1.042), heat 6.06 GJ/t. Lifetime target: keep field fade at the metal-free rate (best measured engineered value 2.2e-3 %/cycle, TDA/GE in lab air). Swing: 25 C/42 Pa to 100 C/1 kPa, steam-assisted, 30-min cycles.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) Airborne Cu ingress (air volume 1,764,780 m3/t, i.e. 81 m3 per kg sorbent per cycle). At 2/5/20 ng/m3 Cu with 100% particle retention, 4 ppm Cu builds up after 24,700/9,900/2,500 cycles, and 20,000 cycles deposit 3.2/8.1/32 ppm. At 10% retention: 0.3-3.2 ppm. This corrects an earlier scratch calculation (durability_ideas.py) that gave 4 ppm in 6-250 cycles because it read ppm as 1e-6 g/kg instead of 1e-3 g/kg, a 1000x slip; its steam figures are right. (2) Steam route: 10 ppb Cu in steam, all deposited, at 1-5x the co-desorbed water (38-188 g per kg per cycle) gives 7.5-38 ppm over 20,000 cycles; 50 ppb at 5x gives 188 ppm. Steam may out-deliver air. (3) Available Fe from dust at 200-1,000 ng/m3 with 1-5% soluble: 3-81 ppm over 20,000 cycles. (4) Converted to first-order rate multipliers vs metal-free (Kuspangaliyeva, 120 C, 4.5 h, dry air): 1.41x at 4 ppm Cu, 2.1-4.2x at about 40 ppm. (5) Levelized model at intrinsic fade 2.2e-3 %/cycle: if metals multiply fade by 1.4/2.1/4.2, the deactivator saves $11/$31/$79 per t. If metals have no effect it costs $2/t. Ligand capacity (1,660 ppm Cu) is 50-500x the projected 20,000-cycle ingress.
ideas.closest_known_work: Min et al., Nat. Commun. 2018: trisodium phosphate chelator plus epoxybutane-PEI, 50x slower deactivation in 15% CO2 flue gas, not shown at 400 ppm. Kuspangaliyeva et al. 2026: shows Cu/Fe sensitivity, offers no in-service fix. Jet-fuel DMD and lubricant benzotriazole/tolyltriazole metal deactivators (not used in sorbents). An earlier scratch sizing in this run of a tethered iminodiacetate/phosphonate chelator did not address redox inertness or the Cu specificity.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Use the Kuspangaliyeva protocol: PEI-800/SBA-15 doped with Cu at 10,000:1 and 1,000:1 (PEI:Cu), with and without 0.5 mol% salicylaldimine, or with tolyltriazole at the same molar level. Include a ligand-only, Cu-free arm. Age 4.5 h at 120 C in dry air, and 18 h at 70 C in humid (43% RH) 0.04% CO2-air. Measure capacity at 30 C and 400 ppm; use UV-vis/EPR to confirm the Cu is held as CuL2 rather than Cu-amine. Pre-stated go: the Cu-doped plus ligand sample keeps within 3 points of the metal-free control (control 72% after 120 C/4.5 h), and the ligand-only sample is no worse than control. Kill: no more than 3 points better than Cu-doped alone, or ligand-only more than 3 points worse (phenol acting as pro-oxidant). In parallel, run ICP-MS on Cu/Fe in a sorbent coupon left at an outdoor air inlet for 3 months and in the steam condensate, to check whether ingress matters at all (the corrosion-coupon approach). Cost: about $2-3k.
ideas.computational_test: Cu speciation with literature stability constants: Cu(II)-polyamine (trien-like) vs Cu(II)-bis(salicylaldiminate) in a matrix with 8-10 mol N/kg and 0.5 mol% ligand. Require at least 99% of Cu in the ligand complex; if not, raise ligand loading or switch to tolyltriazole. Add a Cu(II)/Cu(I) redox-potential estimate for each environment: the ligand must shift E outside the window where ROOH both oxidises and reduces Cu. The ingress and levelized numbers are in section 4 of p2_durability.py.
ideas.conventional_core: PEI (or another polyamine) on silica or alumina, steam-assisted TVSA, field-deployed in dusty air with boiler steam.
ideas.graft: Metal deactivators from jet fuel and lubricants (DMD salicylaldimine, tolyltriazole), which make dissolved Cu catalytically inert at ppm levels.
ideas.why_different: Existing chelator work cleans up metals already in the precursors (phosphate added at synthesis) and was tested in flue gas. This idea is sized and made Cu-specific for metal arriving over 20,000 cycles from steam and dust, costs about 3 cents per kg, and uses a ligand class with decades of service in fuels. It also comes with a test of whether field metal pick-up matters at all; the corrected arithmetic says it can for steam even when airborne dust does not.

ideas.title: Graded bed with a replaceable, cheaper sacrificial inlet cartridge (refinery top-bed skimming applied to DAC contactors)
ideas.one_line: Damage in the field is uneven: the Climeworks/Svante pilot found oxidation stronger on the air-inlet side. So make the most exposed 10-20% of the bed a separate cartridge of cheaper sorbent, swap it on its own schedule, and leave the main bed in service longer.
ideas.mechanism: FTIR on the pilot's post-test sorbent found oxidation more significant on the air-inlet side than on the steam-inlet side (DOE DE-FE0031952 slides, verified text). Every likely cause concentrates at one face: the inlet face meets warm sorbent first when air is readmitted, catches dust and metals, and first absorbs ozone and NOx. Refinery hydrotreaters handle localised fouling with graded beds and skimming of the top layer, replacing a sacrificial guard layer often and the main catalyst rarely. With exponential fade in each zone, a slice that holds a disproportionate share of the damage can be run to a deeper loss (the CO2 front simply moves deeper) and replaced alone. The bulk then lasts much longer, and the slice can be a cheaper sorbent. An optional low-pressure-drop guard pre-layer (activated carbon or a chelating mesh) can also strip particulates, O3 and NOx. If damage is uniform the idea gives nothing, and the model reproduces that.
ideas.key_parameters: Sorbent binding is unchanged (reference dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, working capacity 1.04 mol/kg; swing 25 C/42 Pa to 100 C/1 kPa, 30-min cycles). Bed-average fade 5e-3 %/cycle. Localisation: a fraction g of bed mass (10-20%) carries a share s of the damage (50-80%). Slice sorbent price $8-20/kg; bulk $20/kg. Replacement intervals for slice and bulk are optimised separately. Optional guard layer adds 20-50 Pa.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) Two-zone levelized model (capital $274/t, 60% scaling with mean capacity; optimised whole-bed base $417/t). Uniform damage (g = 0.2, s = 0.2) gives +$0.0, which validates the model. g = 0.20, s = 0.5: -$7/t (same price), -$19/t (slice $8/kg). g = 0.15, s = 0.7: -$23/t and -$33/t; slice replaced every 3,200-6,100 cycles at 53-76% loss, bulk every 15,400-16,300 cycles. g = 0.10, s = 0.8: -$38/t and -$45/t. (2) A guard layer costs 0.059/0.147/0.294 GJ/t of fan electricity for 20/50/100 Pa, i.e. $0.8/$2.0/$4.1 per t at $50/MWh (75% capture, 60% fan efficiency). (3) The idea is worth building only if at least 50% of capacity loss sits in at most 20% of the bed mass.
ideas.closest_known_work: The Climeworks/Svante DOE field pilot autopsy (inlet-side oxidation, qualitative only; no slice-resolved data). Refinery graded guard beds and top-bed skimming. HVAC pre-filters. The map's open problem on graded protection at the evacuation end. No DAC design with a separately replaceable inlet zone was found.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Run a 15-20 cm lab fixed bed of PEI/silica pellets (or a stack of coated sheets) through 50-100 accelerated cycles in the real flow pattern. Feed air at one end with 20 ug/m3 of Cu-bearing test dust; use steam/vacuum regeneration from the other end; readmit air at 60-70 C to exaggerate warm-air contact. Then cut the bed into 8 slices and measure, per slice, 400 ppm capacity, the FTIR 1660 cm-1 band and Cu/Fe by ICP-MS. Pre-stated go: the worst 20% of bed mass holds at least 50% of the capacity loss. Kill: slice-to-slice loss is uniform within +/-20%. The co-location of metals and oxidation also tells apart the dust/metal and warm-air-readmission causes. Cost: about $2-4k. Sectioning a field-aged laminate would be the decisive version.
ideas.computational_test: Build a 1D bed model of a laminate or packed contactor through adsorption, steam heating, evacuation and air readmission. Integrate a piecewise oxidation rate law over each axial slice's temperature and O2 history: about 2% in 18 h at 55 C, 15% in 18 h at 60 C, 17% in 3 h at 70 C, 33% in 24 h at 80 C in air (Li 2024, Guta 2023, Thakkar 2024). Add a particle-deposition profile. This predicts the damage share s for real cycle schedules. Then feed g and s into the graded() optimiser in section 5 of p2_durability.py.
ideas.conventional_core: Structured-laminate or packed-bed solid-amine contactor in steam-assisted TVSA.
ideas.graft: Graded beds with sacrificial guard layers and top-bed skimming from refinery hydrotreating, plus corrosion engineering's practice of designing the wear zone to be replaced.
ideas.why_different: Sorbent cost models assume uniform fade and replace the whole inventory. This idea uses the one field observation of non-uniform oxidation, turns it into a maintenance design with a verifier-backed payoff of $7-45/t, and states the slice-resolved measurement that decides whether it is real. It needs no new chemistry and stacks with every material fix.

ideas.title: Keeping the antioxidant topped up in service: dose a steam-volatile diarylamine radical trap through the regeneration steam
ideas.one_line: Instead of loading a radical trap once and watching it run out, meter ppm levels of diphenylamine (DPA) into the steam that already heats the bed every cycle. The condensing steam carries it into the polymer and holds the stabiliser at a working level for the life of the sorbent, as stored apples are re-fogged with DPA.
ideas.mechanism: Diarylamines are the best stabilisers tested on PEI/Al2O3 (BDDPA: about 1% loss vs 35% after 4.5 h at 120 C in dry air). Protection then collapses: under dry 0.04% CO2-air at 70 C the BDDPA sample went from about 0% loss at 4.5 h to 30% at 18 h (Guta et al. 2025). This is the antioxidant-depletion stage seen in polymer life prediction. Fruit storage solved the same problem: DPA re-applied by thermal fogging after 2-3 months of storage restored residue levels and reduced apple scald (US post-harvest extension and ISHS sources). In steam-assisted TVSA, steam condenses on the cold bed at the start of each heating step, so a steam-volatile antioxidant co-condenses into the sorbent. DPA (bp 302 C) has an estimated vapour pressure of about 91 Pa at 100 C, so ppm-level dosing stays far below saturation. Most of the excess leaves in the condensate and can be recycled. Risks: DPA is weaker than para-substituted diarylamines (para-alkyl analogues are less volatile); NOx can form N-nitrosodiphenylamine; quinone-imine by-products may build up; dosing may be uneven along the bed (deposited at the steam-inlet end first); about 9 ppmv DPA would remain in product CO2 at a 30 C condenser.
ideas.key_parameters: Binding is unchanged (reference dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K). Initial charge: 2 wt% DPA (about 1.5 mol% of N), working capacity 1.021 mol/kg, heat 6.09 GJ/t, work-equivalent 1.89 GJ/t. Steam-assisted TVSA: 25 C/42 Pa to 100 C/1 kPa, about 2-5 mol steam per kg per cycle, 30-min cycles. Dose 11-261 umol DPA per kg per cycle (steam mole fraction 3e-6 to 7e-5). DPA price assumed $4/kg (commodity rubber-chemical intermediate; not verified). Lifetime target: fade from 5e-3 to about 1e-3 %/cycle.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) Dose from site-loss rate / (chain length x stoichiometric factor 2) on a 10.45 mol N/kg sorbent. At fade 5e-3 %/cycle: 0.96/0.32/0.10 kg DPA per t CO2 for chain lengths 1/3/10, i.e. $3.85/$1.28/$0.39 per t. At 2.2e-3: 0.42/0.14/0.04 kg/t ($1.70/$0.57/$0.17). (2) Required steam mole fraction 2.9e-6 to 6.5e-5, against an estimated DPA saturation fraction of 9.0e-4 in 1 atm steam at 100 C (Clausius-Clapeyron from bp with an assumed 62 kJ/mol vaporisation enthalpy). (3) Product-gas carry-over of about 9 ppmv at a 30 C condenser (estimate). (4) Levelized model: fade to 1e-3 with a $1.5-3/t top-up saves $51-52/t vs the $417/t base; fade only to 2e-3 saves $33/t. The top-up costs at most about 7% of the saving.
ideas.closest_known_work: Guta et al., Energy Fuels 2025 (PMC12703673): one-time 2 mol% BDDPA, BTBPA, BTMPS or TTBNB; no replenishment; 1 or 4 mol% no better than 2. Post-harvest DPA thermofogging with re-application during storage of apples. Volatile corrosion inhibitors and boiler-water dosing. An earlier scratch calculation in this run priced DEHA in steam as a scavenger for residual gas-phase O2. No in-service antioxidant replenishment of DAC sorbents was found in a web search.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Run two arms of PEI/Al2O3 with 2 wt% DPA through TGA or small-column cycling: adsorb in humid 0.04% CO2-air at 30 C; regenerate at 100 C in humidified N2; return air at 70 C for 5 min to stress the sorbent. The top-up arm's regeneration gas passes a DPA saturator held to give 10-50 ppm in the vapour; the control arm gets no DPA. Run 60-100 cycles, well past the roughly 18 h of 70 C exposure at which a one-time charge failed. Track capacity every 10 cycles and sorbent DPA content by extraction plus HPLC. Pre-stated go: steady-state DPA of at least 1 mol% of N is held, and fade after cycle 30 is no more than one third of the control's. Kill: fade at least 70% of the control's, or DPA uptake below 0.2 mol% after 20 cycles. The kill result would also show the stabiliser is overwhelmed by radical formation rather than used up, which rules out every top-up strategy. Cost: about $2-3k.
ideas.computational_test: Build a chromatographic transport model of DPA through the bed during steam heating: the condensation front plus a Henry partition between steam and PEI (measure the partition once by headspace GC). Check that at least 80% of bed mass receives a dose within a factor of 2 of target. Then run the dose and levelized calculation (section 6 of p2_durability.py) with the measured partition and chain length from the test.
ideas.conventional_core: Steam-assisted TVSA with diarylamine-stabilised PEI/alumina or silica (the best published additive system).
ideas.graft: In-service antioxidant re-application: DPA thermal fogging of stored apples, and volatile-inhibitor and boiler-water treatment practice.
ideas.why_different: Every published sorbent stabiliser is a one-time charge, and the best one fails once it is depleted. This idea turns the stabiliser into a cheap consumable delivered by a stream the plant already has. Its cost per tonne ($0.2-4/t) is calculated and is small next to the $33-52/t lifetime saving, and a 100-cycle test can decide whether the failure is depletion (fixable) or overwhelm (not).

ideas.title: Ozone-guard face for amine contactors (catalytic deozoniser import)
ideas.one_line: Ambient ozone gives every amine plant a fixed dose of about 1.3e-4 mol O3 per mol CO2 captured, deposited mostly on the air-inlet face. A thin MnOx or carbon ozone-decomposition face, as used in aircraft cabins and HVAC, could remove it for about $1/t, and one cheap dose-response test would show whether ozone is a first-order fade term.
ideas.mechanism: Conventional core: a solid-amine TVSA contactor (PEI/silica, PEI/alumina, Lewatit-type resin or a Svante/Climeworks-type laminate). Imported mechanism (graft): catalytic ozone decomposition on MnOx or Pd/MnO2 honeycombs (aircraft-cabin and photocopier ozone converters) or sacrificial activated-carbon ozone filters (HVAC), placed as a thin face element ahead of the sorbent. Mass balance (executed): the moles of O3 delivered per mole of CO2 captured equal x_O3/(x_CO2 x capture fraction). That number does not depend on sorbent capacity, cycle time or contactor design: 1.27e-4 at 40 ppb and 75% capture. Fractional fade per cycle is therefore Y x 0.0127% at 40 ppb, where Y is the mol of CO2 working capacity destroyed per mol of O3 deposited. The fade budget for a 20,000-cycle life (20% loss) is 1e-3 %/cycle, which ozone alone uses up at Y >= 0.079 (40 ppb) or Y >= 0.105 (30 ppb). Measured field fade (about 3.5e-3 %/cycle) caps Y at about 0.28 if ozone were the only cause. Ozone reacts on first contact, so damage should be front-loaded (mm to cm) on the air-inlet face. That matches the Climeworks/Svante DOE pilot autopsy ('oxidation ... more significant on the air inlet side than steam inlet'), although warm-air re-entry and residual-O2 hypotheses predict the same end, so the axial profile shape must discriminate between them. The earlier upper bound (Jamdade/Sholl 2025, 0.0002 %/cycle) assumed 10 ppb and spread damage over all amines at 25% amine efficiency. At the 20-45 ppb annual-mean background typical of Northern Hemisphere mid-latitudes, and with damage landing on the accessible amines that actually do the CO2 work, the same bound rises about 16x, to about 0.003 %/cycle. Ozone may also initiate radical chains (Y > 1 per site is possible) or be destroyed harmlessly on support or binder (Y small), so only measurement settles it. Secondary point: NO2 at 10-20 ppb in urban air adds a further 0.25-0.5x dose and can nitrosate secondary amines. An alkaline-impregnated layer would be needed for NO2, because MnOx does not remove it.
ideas.key_parameters: Ambient O3 20-45 ppb annual mean (summer afternoons 60-70 ppb); capture fraction 0.75; Y (mol CO2 capacity lost per mol O3 deposited) unknown, plausible 0.01-0.3; O3 deposition fraction in the bed (expected near 1, to be measured); sorbent reference dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, q_max 2 mol/kg, working capacity 1.04 mol/kg, price $20-50/kg; guard: >=90% O3 removal at 50-80% RH, <=20 Pa at 1-2 m/s face velocity, life >=1 year (humid deactivation of MnOx is the known risk; activated carbon is the fallback); guard cost target <=$1/t.
ideas.quantitative_claims: Executed (zeo_graft_calcs.py with climate/physics.py and sorbent.py): (1) O3 delivered per mol CO2 captured is 9.5e-5 / 1.27e-4 / 1.90e-4 at 30 / 40 / 60 ppb, i.e. 2.2 / 2.9 / 4.3 mol (104 / 139 / 208 g) O3 per tonne CO2. (2) Fade = Y x 0.0095 / 0.0127 / 0.019 %/cycle; the whole 20,000-cycle budget (1e-3 %/cycle) is consumed at Y = 0.105 / 0.079 / 0.052. (3) At 40 ppb with Y = 0.1, ozone alone limits life to 15,750 cycles, costing $28/t at $20/kg and $69/t at $50/kg (replacement at 20% loss). Added to a 2.2e-3 %/cycle baseline (TDA/GE-like), a guard is worth $14 / $28 / $55 per tonne at Y = 0.05 / 0.1 / 0.2 ($20/kg sorbent). (4) A 20 Pa guard face adds 0.059 GJ/t of fan electricity (16 kWh/t, $0.8/t at $50/MWh). A stoichiometric sacrificial carbon scavenger needs only about 35 g C per t CO2 at 40 ppb. (5) The published high-dose exposure (IECR 2026: 50 ppm, 50 mL/min, 8 h, 80 mg) equals 0.61 mol O3/kg, about 4,600 cycle-equivalents at 40 ppb if fully absorbed. That paper reports capacity loss for MIL-101(Cr)-PEI, but only in figures and at a single, very high concentration.
ideas.closest_known_work: Jamdade, Cai and Sholl, J. Phys. Chem. C 129, 899 (2025): DFT ozonolysis kinetics for diamine-Mg2(dobpdc) plus an upper-bound estimate at 10 ppb (0.0002 %/cycle, about 8% over 40,000 cycles). Zorrilla-Valtierra, Kuspangaliyeva, Lively, Walton et al., Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2026 (PMC13397569): corona-generated O3/NOx at 50 ppm and above 1,000 ppm on MOF-amines and MIL-101(Cr)-PEI; capacity loss and nitro-group formation, no ppb-level dose-response and no mitigation. Ozone-decomposition catalysts are mature (aircraft cabin converters; Mn/Cu washcoat patent US 6,096,277). A quick literature and patent search found no DAC contactor with an ozone guard (not exhaustive). What is different here: Y is measured at realistic ppb levels and humidity, the dose is framed per tonne independent of capacity (so ozone is a fixed per-tonne cost for every amine design), an axial-profile test is made against the pilot autopsy, and an off-the-shelf guard is proposed.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Bench rig costing about $3-6k: UV-lamp ozone generator, UV-photometric ozone monitor (rented or bought), humidifier and TGA access. Run 0.1-0.5 g PEI/SBA-15 (unprotected) and Lewatit VP OC 1065 in small packed beds at 25 C and 50% RH, with air containing 400 ppm CO2 and O3 at 0.2 ppm and 2 ppm. Log inlet and outlet O3 to get the deposition fraction. Measure 400 ppm CO2 working capacity (TGA or breakthrough) after cumulative doses of 1,000, 3,000 and 10,000 cycle-equivalents (1 cycle-equivalent = 1.27e-4 mol O3 per mol of working capacity). Compute Y. Pre-stated outcomes: kill if Y < 0.02 at both concentrations, because ozone would then be <25% of the fade budget at 40 ppb. Go if Y >= 0.08, because ozone alone would then exceed the budget at 40 ppb; next step is a 1,000 h humid test of a MnOx honeycomb and an activated-carbon face (>=90% removal, <=20 Pa). Validity check: the Y values at the two concentrations must agree within 2x, otherwise accelerated ozone tests cannot be extrapolated.
ideas.computational_test: (a) A plug-flow channel model with reactive-wall uptake (Sherwood number plus uptake coefficient gamma) to predict ozone penetration depth and the axial damage profile for laminate and packed-bed geometries. Compare it with depth-resolved FTIR or N-speciation on a field-aged bed: ozone predicts exponential decay over the first few percent of bed depth, warm-air re-entry predicts a temperature-history profile, and a residual-O2 plug predicts a band at the evacuation end. (b) Integrate hourly ozone records (EPA AQS / EEA) at candidate sites (Iceland, Wyoming, Louisiana, Kenya) into annual dose per kg of sorbent and $/t for a given Y.
ideas.conventional_core: Solid supported-amine TVSA contactor (PEI/silica, PEI/alumina, benzylamine resin or Climeworks/Svante-type laminate).
ideas.graft: Catalytic or sacrificial ozone decomposition face (MnOx or Pd/MnO2 ozone converter from aircraft cabins and photocopiers; activated-carbon ozone filter from HVAC).
ideas.why_different: Oxidation work so far looks at O2 autoxidation during hot steps. Ozone is a separate, cold, per-tonne oxidant. Its dose is fixed by air chemistry, so faster cycling, higher capacity and better antioxidant packages aimed at hot O2 do not reduce it. It can be removed upstream for about $1/t without touching the sorbent chemistry.

ideas.title: Per-cycle oxygen-exposure budget with pump-purge inerting before heating
ideas.one_line: Convert measured PEI oxidation rates into a per-cycle oxygen-exposure budget (kPa·s while the bed is above about 55 C). The budget shows that residual void air at the evacuation depths used in DAC practice can consume the whole 20,000-cycle fade budget. The fix is PSA/vacuum pump-purge inerting (evacuate to <=0.5-2 kPa, or flush the voids with water vapour, before steam enters), and a TGA test can validate the linear-exposure rule.
ideas.mechanism: Conventional core: a steam-assisted temperature-vacuum swing on a supported-amine sorbent.
