Imported mechanism (graft): pump-and-purge inerting and the rinse/equalisation steps used in vacuum and PSA practice to strip light void gas before the product step. Rate law (executed from measured data): continuous exposure of unprotected PEI/gamma-Al2O3 in dry 0.04% CO2 air gives 15% loss per 18 h at 60 C (Li, JACS 2024) and 17% per 3 h at 70 C (Guta, ACS AMI 2023). That is 1.1e-5 and 7.5e-5 % per kPa·s of O2. If damage is linear in exposure, the 1e-3 %/cycle budget allows only about 91 kPa·s per cycle at 60 C or about 13 kPa·s at 70 C for that sorbent. Residual void air when steam is admitted: at 10 kPa evacuation (2.1 kPa O2) with about 60 s hot before it is swept out, exposure is 126 kPa·s, i.e. 1.4e-3 to 9.4e-3 %/cycle (1.4-9x the whole budget). At 2 kPa it is 2.8e-4 to 1.9e-3 %/cycle; at 0.5 kPa, 0.7e-4 to 4.7e-4. Warm-air re-entry (bed at 60-70 C for 60 s in air) is 1,260 kPa·s, or 0.014-0.094 %/cycle (10-100x the budget), which is why cool-before-air matters. A steam condensation front displaces the residual gas plug toward the evacuation port, so the last section of bed heats while still holding O2. This predicts damage concentrated at the evacuation end, consistent with the pilot autopsy wording. Fix: evacuate to <=0.5-2 kPa, or run 1-2 pump-purge flushes with low-pressure water vapour (from a roughly 3 kPa evaporator or the bed's own adsorbed water) before steam; then flash-cool under vacuum to below 50 C before air admission. The energy cost is trivial; the real costs are pump-down time and pump size.
ideas.key_parameters: Void gas volume 1-2.5 L per kg sorbent (packed bed to laminate); evacuation pressure 0.5-10 kPa (DAC patents cite 20-400 mbar); residence of residual O2 above 55 C, 30-120 s; exposure coefficient k(T): 1.1e-5 %/(kPa·s) at 60 C and 7.5e-5 at 70 C (unprotected PEI/Al2O3, dry 0.04% CO2; stabilised sorbents lower, humid conditions higher); oxidation onset 55-60 C; reference sorbent dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, working capacity 1.04 mol/kg; fade budget 1e-3 %/cycle.
ideas.quantitative_claims: Executed (zeo_graft_calcs.py): (1) Residual O2 per cycle is 2.1e-3 mol/kg at 2.5 L/kg void and 10 kPa evacuation (2.0e-3 mol O2 per mol CO2 working capacity), 4.2e-4 at 2 kPa and 1.1e-4 at 0.5 kPa. (2) Allowed exposure for the whole budget: 91 kPa·s per cycle at 60 C, 13 kPa·s at 70 C (unprotected PEI). (3) Exposure and fade: 10 kPa evacuation with 60 s hot gives 126 kPa·s and 1.4e-3 to 9.4e-3 %/cycle; 2 kPa gives 25 kPa·s and 2.8e-4 to 1.9e-3; 0.5 kPa gives 6 kPa·s and 0.7e-4 to 4.7e-4; warm-air re-entry gives 1,260 kPa·s and 0.014-0.094 %/cycle. (4) Vacuum work to evacuate 2.5 L/kg of void gas is at most 0.018 GJ/t (10 kPa), 0.031 (2 kPa) and 0.042 (0.5 kPa), against the 1.88 GJ/t work-equivalent of the reference cycle. (5) Extending sorbent life from 5,000 to 20,000 cycles is worth about $65/t at $20/kg and 1.04 mol/kg (sorbent.py: $87 to $22/t).
ideas.closest_known_work: Li et al., JACS 2024 (PMC11487567) and Guta et al., ACS AMI 2023 measured continuous-exposure kinetics, including the 55-60 C onset and the pro-oxidant effect of 400 ppm CO2. The Climeworks/Svante DOE pilot autopsy found more oxidation on the air-inlet/evacuation side. Climeworks-type patents evacuate to 20-400 mbar before steam. Evaporative vacuum flash cooling is known art (Climeworks, Global Thermostat; the Waseda 2026 multistage steam-recovery simulation). What is different here: a numeric per-cycle O2-exposure budget tied to measured kinetics, applied to the residual-air plug at the start of heating as well as to air re-admission; a quantitative evacuation spec; and a cycle-resolved test of whether short hot O2 pulses obey the same kPa·s law as continuous exposure. The OptiLex map lists a validated rate law on real cycle profiles as an open problem.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: TGA cycling (or a 1 g fixed bed) of unprotected PEI/Al2O3 and of Lewatit VP OC 1065. Each cycle: adsorb 400 ppm CO2 at 50% RH and 25 C, then desorb 30 min at 100 C in N2. Three arms differ only in an O2 pulse at the start of heating: 0, 250 and 2,500 kPa·s per cycle (2 kPa O2 for 125 s; 21 kPa for 120 s). Run 200 cycles per arm (about 100 h of instrument time, under $3k). If the linear rule holds with the 70 C coefficient, expect at least 0.02 and 0.2 %/cycle (about 4% and 37% loss over 200 cycles for the unprotected sorbent). Kill: if the 250 kPa·s arm shows less than 2e-3 %/cycle (exposure coefficient more than 10x below the continuous value, e.g. because of induction-period chemistry), residual void O2 at evacuation depths of 10 kPa or less is not a lever. Go: if fade scales linearly (within 2x) across arms, adopt the evacuation spec (<=2 kPa, or vapour flush) and then test it on a two-bed bench TVSA with an O2 sensor at the outlet.
ideas.computational_test: A 1-D bed model of direct-steam heating that tracks the condensation front, displacement of the residual-gas plug and vacuum-pump capacity. It outputs the O2 partial-pressure and temperature history of each axial slice, integrates k(T)·pO2 into a predicted damage profile, and compares it with the pilot autopsy. Sweep evacuation pressure, pump speed and vapour-flush options to find the cheapest design that keeps exposure under budget.
ideas.conventional_core: Steam-assisted temperature-vacuum swing on a supported-amine sorbent.
ideas.graft: Pump-and-purge inerting and the PSA rinse/depressurisation step that removes light void gas before the product step.
ideas.why_different: The field has focused on air re-admission and on new antioxidant chemistry. This idea quantifies a second oxygen source (the void-air plug at the start of heating) against a measured rate law and finds it is budget-scale at evacuation depths found in practice. The fix is procedural and nearly free in energy, and the same test turns the open rate-law problem into a validated design rule.

ideas.title: Glycine-promoted K2CO3 on mesoporous carbon: amine-free step sorbent
ideas.one_line: Supported K2CO3 already has the right step-shaped thermodynamics for DAC: equilibrium is 1-6 ppm CO2 at 25 C and release is full at 74-98 C under 1-5 kPa vacuum. Its measured uptake is slow. Importing the industrial glycine rate promoter of hot-potassium-carbonate scrubbing into the salt film could give a $4-8/kg, oxidation-free sorbent at about 2 mol/kg.
ideas.mechanism: Conventional core: K2CO3 dispersed on a porous carbon (an existing DAC sorbent class: Twente/Veselovskaya work, K2CO3 on activated carbon and fibre felts). Imported mechanism (graft): the amino-acid rate promoter of the Giammarco-Vetrocoke and Benfield-type hot-potassium-carbonate processes (glycinate or sarcosinate), which catalyses CO2 transfer into concentrated carbonate solution. Thermodynamics (executed, NBS 298 K data): 2KHCO3 -> K2CO3 + CO2 + H2O(g) has dH = 140 kJ/mol (including 1 H2O) and dS = 327 J/mol/K. It is a solid phase change, so uptake is a step rather than a Langmuir curve. Equilibrium CO2 over the anhydrous salt at 25 C is 5.6 / 2.2 / 1.4 ppm at 20 / 50 / 80% RH, so near-complete conversion is possible from 420 ppm (hydrate formation raises this, not computed). Release begins at 74 C (1 kPa CO2 + 1 kPa H2O), 84 C (2 + 2 kPa) and 98 C (5 + 5 kPa), versus 140 C at 1 bar. Working capacity can therefore approach the stoichiometric 2.2-2.9 mol/kg, against 1.04 for the reference amine. Measured bottleneck: 0.11 mmol/g on alumina (inactive K-Al carbonate) and 0.48-0.56 mmol/g on carbons over hours; 40% capacity lost in 50 cycles by K leaching. Film-kinetics estimate (penetration theory): in concentrated carbonate brine at 420 ppm, CO2 transfer is hydration-limited and collapses as the film pH falls. The OH- route gives about 0.18 mmol/g/min early but about 0.014 at 50% conversion (per 10 m2/g of film area). Adding 0.5 M glycinate (k2 about 1.3e4 M-1 s-1) raises this to about 0.9 mmol/g/min. The promoter targets exactly the late-conversion stall that limits measured uptake, and as a hygroscopic co-solute it may keep a thin film below the 43% deliquescence point of K2CO3. The support must be mesoporous with few micropores, because activated-carbon micropores fill with water at about 50-60% RH (a K2CO3/ACF felt lost 40% of its performance when dew point rose from 0 to 12 C).
ideas.key_parameters: 30-40 wt% K2CO3; glycine:K2CO3 0.1-0.2 mol/mol; support: mesoporous or graphitised carbon with water uptake <=0.05 g/g at 80% RH (no alumina or silica, which react with K2CO3); dH 140 kJ/mol (incl. 1 H2O), dS 327 J/mol/K; step 1-6 ppm at 25 C (anhydrous); regeneration 84-98 C at 2-5 kPa CO2 and H2O; conversion per cycle >=90% (unconverted K2CO3 above 43% RH holds >=6.9 mol water per mol, the saturated-solution bound); adsorption step <=60 min; target life >=5,000 cycles; price $4-8/kg (commodity K2CO3 and carbon, assumption).
ideas.quantitative_claims: Executed with sorbent.py helpers (zeo_graft_calcs.py): (1) 30 wt% K2CO3 at 90% conversion: working capacity 1.95 mol/kg; heat 5.17 GJ/t (reaction including 1 H2O 3.18, sensible 0.72 for 25 to 90 C, brine water 0.77, physisorbed water 0.50 assumed); work-equivalent 1.53 GJ/t, versus 1.88 for the reference amine with 2 mol water/mol and 3.01 with the measured 7.6 mol/mol. (2) 40 wt% at 90%: 2.60 mol/kg, 4.99 GJ/t. 40 wt% at 70%: 7.33 GJ/t, with brine water alone 2.96 GJ/t, so >=90% conversion is a hard requirement. If the support carries 3 mol water/mol CO2, add 2.5 GJ/t. (3) Sorbent cost: $23/t at $4/kg and 2,000 cycles, $5/t at 10,000; $47 and $9/t at $8/kg. (4) Capacity of about 2x the reference is the capital lever: the OptiLex tornado gives -$139/t for doubling working capacity. (5) The film model predicts that the unpromoted rate falls more than 10x between 0 and 50% conversion and that the promoter restores it more than 50x.
ideas.closest_known_work: Supported K2CO3 for DAC: Rodriguez-Mosqueda (Twente thesis 2023; 6 wt% on activated-carbon honeycomb, regenerated at 150 C); Veselovskaya et al. (K2CO3/Al2O3, 250-300 C regeneration); Zheng et al. 2024 (K2CO3/AC, 0.562 mmol/g at 5% RH, 40% loss in 50 cycles by leaching); ChemSusChem 2025 (K2CO3 on ACF felt, 0.478 mmol/g in 4 h at 19% RH); Jansuda et al., ACS Omega 2026 (0.11 mmol/g on alumina). Amino-acid-promoted K2CO3 solvents: Melbourne group (glycine, sarcosine and proline promoters, about 22x rate gain with 1 M glycine in 30 wt% K2CO3 at 60 C; glycine-promoted precipitating K2CO3 pilot, flue gas) and the G-V/Benfield processes. A quick search found no amino-acid promoter inside a supported solid K2CO3 sorbent tested at 400 ppm (not exhaustive).
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Incipient-wetness impregnation of a commercial mesoporous carbon with 30 wt% K2CO3, with and without potassium glycinate (glycine:K2CO3 0.15). Test by TGA or a 0.5 g fixed bed at 400 ppm CO2, 25 C, 30% and 60% RH, 120 min. Regenerate at 90 C with >=1-2 kPa CO2 present (vacuum, or a sweep containing 2 kPa CO2), so that release is shown under product-grade conditions rather than an inert purge. Run 50 humid cycles. Materials plus instrument time under $3k. Pre-stated go: the promoted sample reaches >=1.0 mmol/g within 60 min at 60% RH with >=2x the unpromoted initial rate, releases >=80% at <=95 C with >=1 kPa CO2 present, and fades <=10% over 50 cycles. Kill: <0.5 mmol/g in 60 min, or a promoter gain <1.5x, or >20% fade (leaching or glycine decomposition) over 50 cycles.
ideas.computational_test: (a) A penetration-theory film model with promoter kinetics, solved against conversion, pore-filling fraction and RH, to find the film thickness, area and promoter loading at which uptake is no longer hydration-limited. (b) Phase equilibria including K2CO3·1.5H2O and the K4H2(CO3)3·1.5H2O double salt, to pin the real step pressure versus RH. (c) Screen sarcosine, proline, borate and zinc-cyclen mimics by k2, pKa and thermal stability. (d) A step-isotherm adapter for sorbent.py to give cycle heat, work-equivalent and $/t.
ideas.conventional_core: K2CO3 dispersed on a porous carbon support, regenerated by mild temperature-vacuum swing.
ideas.graft: Amino-acid (glycinate/sarcosinate) rate promoter from Giammarco-Vetrocoke and Benfield hot-potassium-carbonate gas treating.
ideas.why_different: It uses the only commodity chemistry in the map whose binding sits inside the useful DAC window as a step. That gives near-stoichiometric swing, no amine to oxidise, and about $4-8/kg. It attacks the specific measured failure (slow late-stage uptake in the salt film) with a promoter proven over decades in industrial carbonate scrubbing, rather than proposing a new framework material.

ideas.title: In-place reductive rejuvenation of oxidised amine sorbents (imine hydrogenation / hydrofinishing import)
ideas.one_line: The Climeworks/Svante pilot found oxidation with no loss of active material, which suggests much of the nitrogen stays in the bed as non-basic imines or Schiff bases. A clean-in-place borohydride wash could turn those back into CO2-active amines for about $1-4/t of reagent, halving sorbent replacement cost if it recovers half the lost capacity.
ideas.mechanism: Conventional core: a PEI-type supported-amine sorbent in a structured contactor. Imported mechanism (graft): reductive restoration of oxidised species, as in refinery hydrofinishing and the imine-hydrogenation step of reductive amination, applied as a periodic liquid wash. Autoxidation converts CH2 next to nitrogen into imines (C=N, weakly basic, CO2-inactive) and amides, and C-N scission makes aldehydes that condense with nearby primary amines into Schiff bases (crosslinks that consume amines). Hydride reduction (NaBH4 in water/methanol at room temperature) converts imines and Schiff bases into secondary amines, which are basic and bind CO2 as carbamate or bicarbonate. Amides, ureas and volatilised fragments are not recovered. The recoverable share therefore equals the imine/Schiff-base share of the damage, which the test measures. Economics (executed): with replacement at 20% loss and a fade of 3.5e-3 %/cycle, sorbent cost falls from $76/t to $53 / $38 / $23 per t if each treatment recovers 30 / 50 / 70% of the lost capacity ($20/kg, 1.04 mol/kg). At 2.2e-3 %/cycle it falls from $48 to $34 / $24 / $14. Reagent at 0.5-2 mol imine per kg with 3x excess is 14-57 g NaBH4 per kg ($0.2-0.85/kg), i.e. $0.9-3.7/t per 5,000-cycle interval. Practical notes at design level: hydrogen release during the wash requires ventilation; borate residue must be rinsed out; the wash fits a clean-in-place step during maintenance.
ideas.key_parameters: Sorbent: PEI/silica, PEI/alumina or laminate (reference dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, working capacity 1.04 mol/kg, $20-50/kg); fraction of oxidative capacity loss present as reducible C=N (unknown, to be measured; target >=30%); reductant 0.05-0.2 M NaBH4, 25 C, about 1 h; 3x stoichiometric excess; treatment every 2,000-5,000 cycles; capacity penalty from borate residue <=2%; post-treatment fade no worse than fresh sorbent.
ideas.quantitative_claims: Executed (zeo_graft_calcs2.py with sorbent.py): (1) Sorbent replacement cost at fade 3.5e-3 %/cycle is $76/t, falling to $53 / $38 / $23 per t for 30 / 50 / 70% recovery per treatment; at 2.2e-3 %/cycle, $48 falling to $34 / $24 / $14. (2) NaBH4 need is 14 / 28 / 57 g per kg sorbent for 0.5 / 1 / 2 mol imine per kg (3x excess), i.e. $0.21 / $0.43 / $0.85 per kg and $0.9 / $1.9 / $3.7 per t CO2 per 5,000-cycle interval at $15/kg reagent. (3) Break-even: the treatment pays if it recovers more than about 5% of lost capacity, because reagent is under $4/t against $48-76/t of replacement cost.
ideas.closest_known_work: Mechanistic oxidation studies identifying imine, amide and carbonyl products: Li et al., JACS 2024; Georgia Tech/LLNL IR and NMR work. Stabilisation rather than repair: epoxide functionalisation plus chelators, Min et al., Nat. Commun. 2018. End-of-life handling: chemical extraction and pyrolysis valorisation of spent PEI/silica (Int. J. Mol. Sci. 2023). The Climeworks/Svante DOE pilot autopsy found oxidation with no loss of active material. A quick search found no report of reductive recovery of oxidised DAC amine sorbents (not exhaustive). What is different here: damage is treated as partly reversible chemistry rather than replacement-only, with a reagent cost about 20x below replacement cost.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Age 2 g of unprotected PEI/SBA-15 (and PEI/Al2O3) in air at 90-100 C until 400 ppm/50% RH capacity is about 50% of fresh. Split the batch: control versus a 0.1 M NaBH4 wash in water/methanol (25 C, 1 h), then rinse and dry at 60 C under N2. Measure 400 ppm/50% RH capacity, CHN, and N speciation by 13C NMR or XPS N1s (imine versus amine versus amide). Repeat the age-and-reduce sequence twice, then run 50 humid TGA cycles. Cost under $2k plus NMR or XPS access. Pre-stated go: >=30% of lost capacity recovered, with fade over the next 50 cycles no worse than fresh sorbent. Kill: <10% recovered, or the recovered capacity lost again within 10 cycles.
ideas.computational_test: Quantify the imine, amide and scission fractions in published spectra of oxidised PEI to bound the recoverable share before any experiment. Use DFT or semi-empirical calculations to compare the H-abstraction barrier of the reduced, crosslinked secondary amines with pristine PEI, to check that repaired sites do not oxidise faster. Run a lifecycle cost model in sorbent.py (fade, recovery fraction, treatment interval).
ideas.conventional_core: PEI-type supported-amine sorbent in a structured TVSA contactor.
ideas.graft: Reductive restoration of oxidised nitrogen species: refinery hydrofinishing and the imine-hydrogenation step of reductive amination, applied as a clean-in-place hydride wash.
ideas.why_different: Every lifetime strategy in the map either prevents oxidation or replaces the sorbent. This one repairs part of the damage in place, using the pilot autopsy observation that the active nitrogen is still present. One small experiment decides it.

ideas.title: Steam and dust deliver oxidation catalysts: FCC-style in-service metal passivation
ideas.one_line: Treat the sorbent like an FCC catalyst that keeps picking up metals in service. Direct steam leaves about 2.5 ppm on the sorbent per ppb of non-volatile impurity over 20,000 cycles, and dust adds more, so Fe and Cu reach 5-120 ppm over life, above the about 4 ppm Cu that measurably speeds PEI oxidation. The fix is periodic re-dosing of a chelating passivator scaled to measured ingress, plus a steam-purity spec.
ideas.mechanism: Conventional core: a steam-assisted TVSA amine contactor in which condensing steam heats the bed and the condensate later evaporates into the air stream. Imported mechanism (graft): FCC metals passivation. Refiners continuously inject a passivator (antimony for nickel, vanadium traps) at a rate proportional to metal input, because the circulating catalyst keeps accumulating metals from the feed and an additive built into fresh catalyst cannot keep up. Evidence that metals matter: Cu and Fe run Fenton-type cycles that initiate amine autoxidation (order Cu > Fe >> Ni). About 4 ppm Cu lowered retained capacity from 72% to 63% after 4.5 h at 120 C in air, and 1000:1 PEI:metal samples retained 25-50% (ES&T 2026). Chelators added at synthesis cannot bind metals that arrive later. Mass balance (executed): the reference cycle condenses about 0.12 kg of steam per kg sorbent per cycle, about 2,500 kg over 20,000 cycles, and non-volatile solutes remain on the sorbent when the condensate evaporates. Steam Fe at 10-50 ppb therefore deposits 25-123 ppm, and Cu at 2-10 ppb deposits 5-25 ppm, over 20,000 cycles. Air contributes 1.6 million m3 per kg sorbent over 20,000 cycles. Urban Cu (10 ng/m3) at 3-30% deposition gives 0.5-5 ppm; Fe at 50-500 ng/m3 gives 2-240 ppm. Spatial check: airborne deposits front-load the air inlet, consistent with the pilot autopsy, whereas steam-borne deposits should be roughly uniform. Steam metals are therefore unlikely to be the main cause in that pilot but set a rising baseline over long life. Passivator stoichiometry is trivial: 20 ppm Cu is 0.31 mmol/kg, while 0.1 wt% phytic acid supplies 1.5 mmol/kg with 6 phosphate groups each.
ideas.key_parameters: Steam purity: Fe 10-50 ppb, Cu 2-10 ppb (assumed range for low-pressure package boilers; to be measured); condensate retained on the bed about 0.12 kg per kg per cycle (all regeneration heat by direct steam, reference cycle); ambient PM metals Cu 1-10 ng/m3, Fe 50-500 ng/m3; deposition fraction in laminates 0.03-0.3 (unknown); passivator (sodium phytate, HEDP or Na3PO4) at 0.1-0.5 wt%, re-dosed every 1,000-5,000 cycles; capacity penalty <=5%; reference sorbent dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, 1.04 mol/kg.
ideas.quantitative_claims: Executed (zeo_graft_calcs2.py): (1) Air processed per kg sorbent is 0.81 million m3 over 10,000 cycles and 1.62 million m3 over 20,000 (75% capture, 1.04 mol/kg). (2) Airborne accumulation over 20,000 cycles: Cu 0.5-4.9 ppm (urban, 3-30% deposited); Fe 2.4-24 ppm (rural PM2.5) or 24-243 ppm (dusty PM10). (3) Direct-steam condensate is 0.123 kg per kg per cycle, so 1 ppb of non-volatile impurity becomes 2.5 ppm on the sorbent over 20,000 cycles. Fe at 10 / 50 ppb gives 24.6 / 122.8 ppm; Cu at 2 / 10 ppb gives 4.9 / 24.6 ppm. (4) These levels match or exceed the about 4 ppm Cu (10,000:1) that measurably raised oxidative loss and approach the 1,000:1 ratio (about 40 ppm) that cut retention to 25-50% (ES&T 2026, 120 C dry-air test). (5) 20 ppm Cu = 0.31 mmol/kg, against 1.5 mmol/kg of phytate at 0.1 wt%.
ideas.closest_known_work: Min et al., Nat. Commun. 2018: trisodium phosphate chelator on silica plus epoxybutane-PEI, about 50x slower deactivation, but at flue-gas conditions and added only at synthesis. Kuspangaliyeva, Lively and Jones, ES&T 2026 (PMC13235560): metal-doping series, Cu > Fe >> Ni; names steam and dust as possible sources. Industrial precedent: FCC Ni/V passivation (antimony injection, vanadium traps) and power-plant condensate polishing and steam-purity limits. What is different here: a per-cycle ingress mass balance showing that direct steam makes the bed a residue collector for steam impurities, an in-service rather than synthesis-only passivation strategy, and a spatial test that separates airborne from steam-borne metal.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: (1) ICP-MS of condensate from a lab or pilot steam generator, and of fresh versus field-aged sorbent if any is obtainable (about $50 per sample). (2) Make PEI/SBA-15 and PEI/Al2O3 with post-deposited metals applied by aqueous spray and drying to mimic condensate: Cu at 0, 5 and 20 ppm, Fe at 0 and 50 ppm. Test each with and without a post-dosed 0.3 wt% sodium phytate (or Na3PO4) spray. Age 18 h at 70 C in humid (50% RH) 0.04% CO2 air and measure 400 ppm capacity. About $2-3k. Pre-stated go: post-deposited Cu <=20 ppm or Fe <=50 ppm raises loss >=1.5x versus metal-free, and post-dosing recovers >=80% of that difference with <=5% loss of fresh capacity. Kill: these metal levels change loss by less than 1.2x, or ICP-MS shows steam Fe <1 ppb and Cu <0.2 ppb (lifetime deposition under 2.5 and 0.5 ppm).
ideas.computational_test: Site-specific ingress model combining PM speciation data (EPA CSN, EEA), size-resolved particle deposition in 1 mm laminate channels (diffusion and impaction) and measured steam purity, giving ppm per cycle by bed depth. Couple it to a metal-dependent oxidation rate law fitted to ES&T 2026 data, to rank steam polishing, a particle pre-filter and passivator dosing by $/t.
ideas.conventional_core: Steam-assisted TVSA supported-amine contactor with direct steam condensation on the bed.
ideas.graft: FCC-style continuous metals passivation: passivator dosed in service in proportion to metal ingress.
ideas.why_different: Stabilisation work adds a chelator once, at synthesis, and tests clean materials. This idea shows that the plant itself keeps delivering ppm-level catalytic metals, mainly through retained steam condensate and front-loaded dust, so passivation has to be replenished in service like FCC catalyst management, and steam purity becomes a sorbent-lifetime specification.

ideas.title: Strip-and-reimpregnate: ex-situ catalyst-style rejuvenation of structured amine sorbents
ideas.one_line: Separate the expensive structure from the cheap amine. When a structured sorbent fades, acid-strip the oxidised polymer and reload fresh PEI, as refiners do with ex-situ rejuvenation of hydrotreating catalysts. At about $5/kg per refresh, this cuts sorbent replacement from $87 to $41/t (5,000-cycle life, $20/kg laminate) or from $218 to $69/t ($50/kg).
ideas.mechanism: Conventional core: a PEI-impregnated silica (or alumina) structured sorbent: laminate, monolith washcoat or pellets. Imported mechanism (graft): ex-situ catalyst rejuvenation (the Eurecat, Porocel and Albemarle model). The spent catalyst is stripped of deactivating deposits and reloaded with active phase, and the support and shaping (the costly part) are reused several times. For sorbents: protonate and dissolve the oxidised PEI and its fragments with dilute acid in water/methanol, rinse, and re-impregnate fresh PEI to the original pore-fill fraction. Assumptions (stated): amine 40 wt% at $5/kg ($2/kg of sorbent), processing $3/kg, the support survives 5 refreshes (so its cost is amortised over 5 lives), and refreshed capacity is 95% of fresh. This complements the in-place reductive idea: it covers damage that hydride cannot repair (amides, urea crosslinks, chain scission, lost fragments). It fails if oxidised PEI crosslinks into an insoluble network that blocks the mesopores.
ideas.key_parameters: New structured sorbent $20-50/kg; amine fraction 40 wt%, PEI $5/kg (assumption); stripping 0.1 M HCl in water/methanol at 25-50 C; processing $3/kg (assumption); support reuse 5 times; capacity recovery >=90-95%; residual organic after strip <=3 wt%; pore-volume recovery >=90%; life per charge 2,000-10,000 cycles; reference sorbent dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, 1.04 mol/kg.
ideas.quantitative_claims: Executed (zeo_graft_calcs.py, sorbent_cost_per_tonne): replace versus rejuvenate at $20/kg new laminate is $218 versus $103/t (2,000 cycles), $87 versus $41/t (5,000) and $44 versus $21/t (10,000). At $50/kg it is $545 versus $172/t, $218 versus $69/t and $109 versus $34/t. The saving is 2-3x at every lifetime and grows with the price of the structured support. Above about $20/kg, rejuvenation is worth more per tonne than a further 2x lifetime gain on a non-rejuvenated sorbent.
ideas.closest_known_work: Chemical extraction of PEI from spent PEI/silica and pyrolysis valorisation with silica recovery (Int. J. Mol. Sci. 2023, end-of-life rather than closed-loop reuse with capacity data); recovery of K2CO3/activated carbon capacity by re-impregnation after leaching (Zheng et al. 2024); ex-situ catalyst rejuvenation industry practice. What is different here: a closed-loop refresh of oxidatively aged structured DAC sorbents with pre-stated pore-volume and capacity recovery criteria, and economics run through the OptiLex sorbent verifier. It turns sorbent cost into roughly amine price plus processing.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Age PEI-impregnated SBA-15 or silica gel (40 wt% PEI), and if available a PEI/silica laminate coupon, to about 50% of fresh 400 ppm/50% RH capacity at 100 C in air. Strip with 0.1 M HCl in 1:1 water/methanol, then rinse with water and methanol. Measure residual C and N (CHN) and N2-physisorption pore volume. Re-impregnate fresh PEI to the original loading and measure capacity. Repeat age, strip and reload 3 times. Cost under $1.5k. Pre-stated go: after the second refresh, >=90% of fresh capacity, >=90% of the original pore volume and <=3 wt% residual organic. Kill: <80% capacity recovery or <80% pore volume, meaning oxidised polymer is insoluble or crosslinked in the pores, or laminate binder or backing damaged by the strip.
ideas.computational_test: Lifecycle cost model in sorbent.py with support degradation per refresh, recovery fraction, processing cost and downtime, compared with the replacement baseline and with the in-place reductive treatment. Extend NETL-style plant cost models to include a refresh logistics loop (swap-out modules, central rejuvenation facility).
ideas.conventional_core: PEI-impregnated silica or alumina structured sorbent (laminate, monolith washcoat or pellets).
ideas.graft: Ex-situ catalyst rejuvenation: strip deactivating deposits and reload the active phase on the reused support and shaped body.
ideas.why_different: Published sorbent economics assume the whole structured sorbent is replaced at end of life, which ties $/t to $15-100/kg structured-sorbent prices. Catalyst-industry practice decouples the two. The pass/fail criterion (pore volume and capacity after repeated strips) is a one-month bench experiment.

ideas.title: Acid-gas lifetime floor, tested and guarded by a bicarbonate scavenger layer
ideas.one_line: Ambient ppb SO2, HNO3 and HCl react irreversibly with amine and quaternary-ammonium sites. By calculation this alone can use up the whole 20,000-cycle fade budget in suburban air. A cheap bicarbonate/carbon guard layer upstream should remove it for under $2/t; a 6-day dosing experiment can confirm or kill the idea.
ideas.conventional_core: Solid-amine TVSA bed (PEI or benzylamine type; reference dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, q_max 2 mol/kg), or a quaternary-ammonium moisture-swing bed, fitted with an ordinary particle pre-filter.
ideas.graft: Scavenger/guard-bed practice from ion-exchange water demineralisation: a sacrificial layer upstream of the working resin takes up irreversible poisons. Here it is a thin bicarbonate-form layer, such as NaHCO3 or KHCO3 on activated-carbon cloth or a carbonate-form commodity anion resin felt, that neutralises strong acid gases before they reach the CO2 sorbent. The carbon also decomposes O3 and part of the NO2.
ideas.mechanism: Strong acids carried by the air (SO2 oxidised to sulfite/sulfate, HNO3, HCl, part of NO2) form heat-stable ammonium salts or sulfonamides on primary and secondary amines. Neither steam nor a 100 C vacuum swing reverses them. On quaternary-ammonium resins the anions (nitrate, sulfate, chloride) displace carbonate for good. The number of acid equivalents taken up per mol of CO2 captured is fixed by the air composition, about 3.0e-6 per ppb, and does not depend on sorbent capacity or cycle speed. So higher capacity or faster cycling cannot outrun it. Only exclusion or reversibility helps. The guard works because strong acids displace CO2 from bicarbonate (HNO3 + NaHCO3 -> NaNO3 + CO2 + H2O). Once the guard is in bicarbonate form it takes up no net CO2, and it captures the acid front within millimetres. This also predicts that the amine bed is damaged most at the air inlet, which matches the inlet-side oxidation seen in the Climeworks/Svante pilot autopsy. That pattern is a confound to test, not proof.
ideas.key_parameters: Amine core: dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, q_max 2 mol/kg, working capacity 1.04 mol/kg (OptiLex reference), N inventory about 10 mol N/kg for 45 wt% PEI. Moisture-swing core: about 0.5 CO2 per N+ (carbonate/bicarbonate swing). Acid capture fraction assumed 95% (results scale linearly). Ambient strong-acid load 1-14 ppb-eq: rural US 2022-24 CASTNET total nitrate 0.6-1.2 ug/m3 (about 0.25-0.5 ppb); suburban 3-4; industrial or port 8-14. Guard: 1.5-3 eq/kg usable capacity, $2-5/kg, 10-20 Pa pressure drop, single use, swapped like a filter element outside the vacuum chamber. Lifetime target 20% loss over 20,000 cycles (1.1e-3 %/cycle). Sorbent at $20-50/kg.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) Air per tonne CO2 at 75% capture is 1.76e6 m3. 1 ppb of strong acid captured at 95% gives 0.069 eq per t CO2, i.e. 3.0e-6 eq per mol CO2. That neutralises 3.0e-4 % of working sites per cycle per ppb-eq (severe bound: acids take working sites 1:1). (2) Expected rates: rural 2.7-3.6e-4 %/cycle; suburban 8.4e-4 to 1.1e-3 (equal to the whole 1.1e-3 budget); industrial/port 2.6-4.1e-3; an illustrative 10 ppb SO2-equivalent geothermal case 3.2-6.2e-3. Acid-only life to 20% loss: 17,000-24,000 cycles suburban, 4,900-7,800 industrial. The mild bound, where acids neutralise random N among 10 mol N/kg, is 10x lower. (3) For a quaternary-ammonium moisture-swing bed the rates are half the amine values (0.5 CO2 per N+). (4) Expected sulfur after 10,000 cycles at 1 ppb SO2 is 30 mmol/kg (0.1 wt% S), easily measured. (5) Guard needs 46-548 g per t CO2 for 2-12 ppb-eq, costing $0.2-1.4/t. Fan work at 10-20 Pa is 0.03-0.06 GJ/t ($0.4-0.8/t at $50/MWh). (6) If 1.0e-3 of the measured 2.2e-3 %/cycle fade is acid-driven, the guard cuts sorbent cost from $53 to about $29/t at $20/kg and 1.04 mol/kg (saving about $24/t), and saves about $60/t at $50/kg. The saving is larger for $50-200/kg MOFs and COFs. (7) Confound: the best multi-thousand-cycle fade (TDA/GE, 2.2e-3 %/cycle) was measured in indoor lab air, where acid gases are depleted, so it may understate field fade. Scripts: climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/ionex_pass2.py and ionex_pass2b.py.
ideas.closest_known_work: Hengst sells a DAC pre-filter described as optimised for acid gases (https://www.hengst.com/en/products/productgroups/39-air-filtration-industries/1704-filters-for-direct-air-capture-systems/1706-pre-filter-for-direct-air-capture-systems). It is a company product with no published performance data. KAIST built an SO2-resistant amine adsorbent with a tertiary-amine surface layer for flue gas (dspace.kaist.ac.kr/handle/10203/262422). GE/Alstom patent US9101912 regenerates SO2/NOx-deactivated solid amines by NaOH washing (flue gas, 2012). Guard-bed patents such as US5443623. Jamdade/Cai/Sholl 2025 DFT bound for ozone at 2e-4 %/cycle. I found no public DAC study that budgets ppb acid gases against the per-cycle fade target.
ideas.why_different: Existing work treats SO2 as a flue-gas problem at ppm levels, and the DAC pre-filter has no published data. The calculation here shows that at ppb levels acid uptake is a per-tonne-of-CO2 loss: about 3e-4 %/cycle per ppb-eq, independent of capacity and cycle rate. It is the same size as the measured fade of engineered sorbents. The proposed test measures the one missing number that decides whether guards matter: working sites lost per acid equivalent.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Accelerated acid dosing on 1 g of PEI/gamma-Al2O3 (or Lewatit VP OC 1065) at 25 C, 50% RH, 400 ppm CO2, 1 L/min per g. Spike 100 ppb SO2 (or HNO3/HCl from permeation tubes) for 5.6 days, which equals 10,000 cycles at 1 ppb-eq. Run about 20 TVSA cycles per day (100 C, N2 or vacuum) throughout. Measure CO2 capacity by TGA and retained S/N/Cl by combustion analysis and IC of a water extract. Pre-stated thresholds: the idea stands if at least 80% of the dosed acid stays bound after regeneration and at least 0.5 working CO2 site is lost per equivalent. It is falsified if fewer than 0.1 sites are lost per equivalent, which means acids are not a lifetime term in DAC. Guard arm: a 2 mm NaHCO3-on-carbon-cloth layer upstream must remove at least 90% of SO2 and HNO3 at no more than 20 Pa and 1 m/s face velocity, and the protected bed must retain at least 2x more capacity than the unprotected one. Cost about $3-5k (permeation tubes, SO2 analyser rental, IC/CHNS analyses). If field-aged sorbent is available, an axial S/NO3/Cl profile costs a few hundred dollars and tests the inlet-side pattern directly.
ideas.computational_test: Multiply gridded reanalysis fields of SO2, HNO3 and HCl (e.g. CAMS or EPA CMAQ) by 3.0e-4 %/cycle per ppb-eq to map acid-limited sorbent life by candidate DAC site. Then couple an acid-uptake front to a 1-D bed model to predict the axial capacity-loss profile and compare it with the Climeworks/Svante inlet-versus-steam-side autopsy.

ideas.title: Ammonia emission rate as a 100-cycle sorbent fade meter
ideas.one_line: Import the fuel-cell fluoride-emission-rate method: measure the NH3 and volatile amines a sorbent releases per cycle and use that as the degradation rate. This could resolve fade of about 1e-3 %/cycle in 2-160 cycles instead of the 2,000-6,000 cycles capacity tracking needs.
ideas.conventional_core: Standard accelerated ageing of supported amines: TGA and small fixed beds, using Li 2024 (18 h, 0.04% CO2 air), Guta 2023/2025 (70-120 C, dry and humid) and humid 400 ppm cycling.
ideas.graft: PEM fuel-cell accelerated stress testing, where the membrane chemical degradation rate is read from the fluoride emission rate in effluent water at ppb sensitivity rather than waiting for failure. Here the effluent marker is NH4+ and volatile amines for PEI-type sorbents, and trimethylamine for quaternary-ammonium moisture-swing resins.
ideas.mechanism: Oxidative C-N scission of aminopolymers releases NH3 and low-molecular-weight amines (HR-ToF-CIMS and PTR-MS studies have detected them). If the NH3 released per lost working site (Y) is roughly constant across conditions, the cumulative NH3 trapped from exhaust and condensate is a direct integral of fade. Ion chromatography detects nmol quantities. Capacity measurements carry 1-3% scatter, so they can only resolve small per-cycle fades after thousands of cycles. The marker therefore turns lifetime ranking from a months-long measurement into a days-long one, for every stabiliser idea in the engine.
ideas.key_parameters: Sorbent: 45 wt% PEI on gamma-Al2O3 (fresh about 1.3 mmol/g; reference working capacity 1.04 mol/kg, dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K). Target fade resolution 1e-3 %/cycle. NH3 yield Y per lost working site 0.01-1, unknown and calibrated by the test. Sample 1-10 g. IC detection limit 0.01 mg/L NH4+ in a 10 mL dilute-acid trap (5.5 nmol). Marker for quaternary-ammonium resins: trimethylamine. Equipment cost under $5k.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) At 1e-3 %/cycle and wc 1.04 mol/kg, sites lost are 1.04e-8 mol per g per cycle. With Y 0.03-1 and a 10 g sample: 3-104 nmol NH3 per cycle, reaching 3x the IC detection limit in 1-6 cycles. With 1 g at Y 0.01: 160 cycles. (2) Capacity-based detection of the same fade needs 2,000 cycles at +/-1% scatter and 6,000 at +/-3%. (3) The Climeworks/Svante autopsy found oxidation without loss of active material, which suggests Y may be small (0.01-0.1); the calculation shows that is still workable at 10 g scale. (4) Ranking power: stabiliser candidates (BDDPA, thioethers, chelators, items 3-6 of this set) could each be scored in about 50 cycles instead of 5,000+. Script: climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/ionex_pass2.py and ionex_pass2b.py.
ideas.closest_known_work: PEMFC fluoride emission rate and the DOE OCV-hold accelerated stress test. Product identification for oxidised PEI by Georgia Tech/LLNL (HR-ToF-CIMS, AIChE 2022 592b; ACS AMI 2023, doi 10.1021/acsami.3c08140) and WashU work on emissions from CO2 removal (environment.washu.edu/xu-emissions-from-co2-removal-2) identify NH3 and amines but treat them as emissions or mechanism clues, not as a calibrated rate meter. The OptiLex map lists battery-style off-gas metrology as an open problem with no prior-art check.
ideas.why_different: It turns degradation products from a curiosity or emissions issue into a quantitative fade-rate instrument. The proportionality test (constant Y across conditions) is stated before the experiment, so the method can fail cleanly.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Cycle 10 g of PEI/gamma-Al2O3 (plus one BDDPA-stabilised arm) in a fixed bed under 4 conditions: dry vs 50% RH, and air readmission at 70 C vs 100 C. Run 50 cycles each, with all exhaust and desorption condensate bubbled through 10 mL of 1 mM H2SO4 traps that are changed every 10 cycles. Measure NH4+ and C1-C2 amines by IC, and CO2 capacity by TGA every 10 cycles and at the end. Compute Y as NH3 released per working site lost. Pre-stated: the metric is validated if Y stays within 2x across all 5 condition/material arms and the NH3-rate ranking matches the capacity-loss ranking (Spearman 1.0 on 5 arms). It is falsified if Y varies more than 3x, or if the stabilised arm cuts capacity loss but not NH3 rate, or the reverse. Cost about $3k.
ideas.computational_test: Fit a two-pathway mass balance (C-N scission releasing NH3 versus in-place amide/imine formation releasing nothing) to published product distributions for PEI at 70-120 C, and predict how Y should change with temperature and humidity before the experiment.

ideas.title: Ion-exchange polishing of native and steam-borne Cu/Fe in PEI sorbents
ideas.one_line: Commercial PEI already carries about 5-20x the 4 ppm Cu shown to accelerate oxidation, and steam and dust can add a similar amount over one sorbent life. Strip it with chelating ion exchange (as in chlor-alkali brine and condensate polishing) and keep the regeneration steam polished.
ideas.conventional_core: PEI impregnated on mesoporous silica or gamma-alumina, regenerated by steam-assisted TVSA.
ideas.graft: Chelating ion-exchange polishing from chlor-alkali membrane-cell brine treatment and power-plant condensate polishing. The PEI feed is acidified so its amines release bound metals, passed through an aminophosphonate or bis-picolylamine chelating resin, and returned to free-base form on an OH-form anion resin, which leaves no salt. The same polishing is applied to regeneration-steam condensate.
ideas.mechanism: Cu(II)/Cu(I) and Fe(III)/Fe(II) decompose hydroperoxides by Fenton-type cycles and start amine autoxidation chains. At neutral pH PEI chelates these metals more strongly than most resins, so it holds its own impurities. Protonating the amines (pH about 2-3) releases them. The resin captures them. The OH-form anion exchanger then swaps Cl- for OH-, giving metal-free, salt-free PEI. In-situ chelators such as phosphate passivate metals but leave them in place and cannot keep up with metals arriving in service. Removal plus a steam/condensate purity specification limits the total metal load over the sorbent's life.
ideas.key_parameters: Amine reference: dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, q_max 2 mol/kg, wc 1.04 mol/kg, 100 C, 1 kPa CO2, 2 mol water per mol CO2 (6.04 GJ/t). As-made metal: commercial PEI 7-160 ppm Fe and up to 47 ppm Cu, i.e. up to 21 ppm Cu and 3-72 ppm Fe on the sorbent at 45 wt% PEI. Target under 1 ppm Cu and Fe. Steam 2 t per t CO2 with 1-10 ppb Cu (assumed range). Dust Cu 2-50 ng/m3 with 10-30% deposition (assumed). Chelating resin need 0.33 g per kg sorbent. Lifetime 9,000-20,000 cycles.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) As-made sorbent can already hold up to about 21 ppm Cu and 3-72 ppm Fe. A 120 C, 4.5 h air test showed about 4 ppm Cu cutting retained capacity from 72% to 63% (Kuspangaliyeva/Lively/Jones ES&T 2026). (2) Ingress over one life (9,091 / 20,000 cycles; 416 / 915 kg CO2 per kg sorbent): steam with 1-10 ppb Cu at full retention adds 0.8-8.3 / 1.8-18 ppm Cu. Urban dust (20 ng/m3, 20% deposited) adds 2.9 / 6.5 ppm (bed average; the inlet face will be higher). Rural dust adds under 0.3 ppm. Traffic-heavy sites add 11-24 ppm. (3) So purification is the first-order lever, and it lasts a full life only if steam is held below about 1 ppb Cu and the site is not traffic-heavy. (4) Resin cost is about $0.005 per kg sorbent; the real costs are the acidify and free-base steps. (5) If native metals double the fade rate (2.2e-3 versus 1.1e-3 %/cycle), sorbent cost falls from $53 to $27/t at $20/kg and from $134 to $67/t at $50/kg (OptiLex sorbent_cost_per_tonne, 20% end-of-life). Script: climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/ionex_pass2.py.
ideas.closest_known_work: Kuspangaliyeva, Lively, Jones, ES&T 2026 (PMC13235560): deliberate Cu/Fe/Ni doping of PEI/SBA-15; it notes most studies only report pre-existing metals. Yan and Sayari doped supports with Fe/Cu. Min et al., Nat. Commun. 2018: trisodium phosphate chelator plus epoxybutane, about 50x slower deactivation in flue gas. Isenberg and Chuang reported Cu, Fe and Zn in boiler steam accelerating amine degradation. AIChE 2024-25 talks on metal contaminants in DAC sorbents. No published removal of native metals from commercial PEI, and no lifetime ingress budget, was found.
ideas.why_different: Prior work adds metals to show harm, or adds chelators that leave metals in place. This idea removes them with a standard ion-exchange sequence and adds a numerical ingress budget (steam plus dust). The budget says how clean the steam must be and where purification pays.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Purify 50 g of PEI 800 (acidify with HCl, chelating resin column, OH-form strong-base resin) and verify by ICP-MS that Cu and Fe are below 1 ppm. Make 35 wt% sorbents on low-metal SBA-15 from purified PEI, as-received PEI, and as-received PEI plus 2 wt% Na3PO4. Run three protocols: 4.5 h at 120 C in dry air; 18 h at 70 C in dry 0.04% CO2 air; 30 humid TGA cycles (adsorb 400 ppm at 50% RH and 30 C, desorb at 100 C, 20 min air at 70 C each cycle). Pre-stated: the idea stands if purified PEI loses no more than two-thirds of the as-received loss (1.5x slower) in at least 2 of 3 protocols. It is falsified if the difference is under 1.2x in all three, which would mean native metals are not rate-setting. Ingress check: 200 cycles with 500 ppb Cu dosed into the steam-generator water (100x accelerated) should give about 9 ppm Cu by ICP-MS if retention is near 100%. Cost about $3-4k.
ideas.computational_test: Combine site-specific dust-metal data and a steam-chemistry assumption with a Fenton-initiation rate law fitted to the Kuspangaliyeva dose series (1:1 to 100,000:1 PEI:metal) to predict fade versus cycle number for purified and as-received sorbent at candidate sites.

ideas.title: Steam-borne replenishable radical trap for solid amines
ideas.one_line: Dose a volatile, acid-free hydroxylamine oxygen scavenger and radical trap, as used in boiler and thermal-desalination feedwater, into the regeneration steam, so the solid amine is re-protected every cycle just before hot sorbent meets air.
ideas.conventional_core: Steam-assisted TVSA of a PEI-type or benzylamine solid sorbent at about 100 C (reference dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, q_max 2 mol/kg, wc 1.04 mol/kg).
ideas.graft: Volatile oxygen-scavenger dosing from boiler and thermal-desalination feedwater conditioning (DEHA, N-isopropylhydroxylamine). These hydroxylamines travel with steam and are also radical short-stops in emulsion polymerisation. Here a few to about 100 ppm in the regeneration steam or in the humid purge during cool-down replaces a fixed antioxidant that is used up and cannot be topped up in service.
ideas.mechanism: N-alkylhydroxylamines have a weak O-H bond. They donate H to peroxyl radicals and form nitroxides that then trap alkyl radicals, breaking the autoxidation chain that starts when sorbent above about 55-60 C meets air. Additives blended in at synthesis (BDDPA, hindered amines, thioethers) are consumed, block amine sites, and fade within tens of hours in humid 0.04% CO2 air. Steam delivery replaces the trap every cycle, puts it where steam condenses (throughout the bed), and needs no change to the sorbent. Leftover scavenger and its oxime/ketone products leave with the air or condensate. The key chemical risk is that some hydroxylamines (DEHA) end as carboxylic acids, which would form heat-stable salts on the amine. Hence N-isopropylhydroxylamine is preferred: its oxidation gives acetone and acetone oxime, not acids.
ideas.key_parameters: Steam 2 t per t CO2, i.e. 92 g steam per kg sorbent per cycle. Measured engineered-sorbent fade 2.2e-3 %/cycle (TDA/GE). Radical-chain length 1-10 (assumed). 2 radicals trapped per molecule. Retention 10-100%. Dose 1-111 ppm in steam. Scavenger price about $6/kg. The acid by-product must stay below 0.2 mol retained carboxylic acid per mol dosed. Damage window: air contact above 55-60 C (Li et al. JACS 2024: 2% loss at 55 C vs 15% at 60 C in 18 h).
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) Trap demand at 2.2e-3 %/cycle: 1.1e-6 to 1.1e-5 mol per kg per cycle (chain length 10 to 1). That is 1-111 ppm in steam for 100% to 10% retention, 2-223 g per t CO2, and $0.01-1.34/t at $6/kg. (2) Average exhaust concentration if all of it is vented with the air: 1-126 ug/m3 (needs emissions review). (3) An unprotected PEI fading at 1.6 %/cycle would need 1.6-16 kg per t CO2, so the method only suits already-engineered sorbents. (4) Acid by-product risk: if each dosed DEHA left one carboxylic acid on the amine (chain 10, 10% retention dose), it would neutralise 1.1e-3 % of working sites per cycle, equal to the whole lifetime budget. This sets the kill criterion and the choice of N-isopropylhydroxylamine. (5) Value: halving fade from 2.2e-3 to 1.1e-3 %/cycle cuts sorbent cost from $53 to $27/t at $20/kg and from $134 to $67/t at $50/kg (OptiLex sorbent_cost_per_tonne, 1.04 mol/kg, 20% end-of-life). Scripts: ionex_pass2.py and ionex_pass2b.py in climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/.
ideas.closest_known_work: University of Regina patent WO2009065218 (2008): hydroxylamine (0.025-1 kmol/m3), sulfite, EDTA and tartrate as oxidation inhibitors in liquid MEA for flue-gas capture. DEHA as a volatile boiler oxygen scavenger and gas-treating vapour-phase O2 scavenger (patent literature). Guta et al., Energy & Fuels 2025 (PMC12703673): BDDPA, hindered amines and spin traps blended into PEI/Al2O3, with the benefit fading in humid 0.04% CO2 air. No solid-sorbent DAC study delivering an antioxidant through the regeneration steam was found.
ideas.why_different: Liquid-amine inhibitors are dissolved once in a circulating solvent. Solid DAC sorbents cannot be topped up, so every published stabiliser is a one-time charge. Using the steam that already contacts the whole bed every cycle as the delivery route is new. The per-cycle demand and the acid by-product limit are computed in advance.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: 1 g fixed bed or TGA of PEI/gamma-Al2O3 (plus one Lewatit arm). Each cycle: adsorb 400 ppm CO2 at 50% RH and 30 C for 30 min; desorb at 98-100 C in steam or wet N2 made from water containing 0, 50 or 500 ppm N-isopropylhydroxylamine (and DEHA as comparator); readmit air at 75 C for 10 min (deliberate stress); cool. Run 100 cycles. Measure capacity every 10 cycles. At the end, IC of a water extract for acetate, formate, nitrite and nitrate. Pre-stated: the idea stands if the dosed arm loses no more than 50% of the control's capacity loss after 100 cycles and retained carboxylic acid is no more than 0.2 mol per mol dosed. It is falsified if the reduction is under 25%, or if retained acid exceeds 0.5 mol per mol dosed. Cost about $3k (syringe pump, TGA or bed time, IC).
ideas.computational_test: Add a trap term (k_trap[ROO*][AH], with replenishment pulses at each steam step) to a cycle-resolved autoxidation kinetic model fitted to Li 2024 and Guta 2023 data, to find the minimum dose and the best dosing moment (end of steam versus cool-down purge).

ideas.title: Metered low-wet-pickup wetting for moisture-swing sheets
ideas.one_line: Replace immersion wetting of moisture-swing resin (about 100 kg water per kg CO2) with textile foam or kiss-roll application at 0.4-0.6 g/g. This brings water use down to vapour-wetting levels while keeping liquid-contact release speed, and removes drying as the step that limits the cycle.
ideas.conventional_core: Quaternary-ammonium anion-exchange moisture-swing sorbent (IRA-900 or Excellion-type sheet, carbonate/bicarbonate swing, 0.68-1.27 mol/kg working capacity) that loads CO2 in dry air and releases it when wetted.
ideas.graft: Low-wet-pickup liquor application from textile finishing: foam or kiss-roll application at a few tens of percent wet pickup instead of padding or immersion at 70-100% or more. Textile finishers developed it to cut the drying load. Here it doses only the water the resin's hydration shell needs.
ideas.mechanism: CO2 release needs the exchange sites to reach high water activity (about 0.9-1.0). Water beyond the resin's own hydration capacity, such as interstitial and mesh-held liquid in packets (3.3 g/g measured, mesh alone 57 wt%), adds nothing to release. It still has to evaporate before the sorbent can take up CO2 again; the ASU wind-tunnel data show 30 min of drying before any CO2 binds. Applying a metered liquid dose near the resin's saturated hydration (about 0.4-0.6 g/g) wets the sites in seconds, with liquid contact rather than slow vapour diffusion. It caps evaporation per CO2 near the vapour-wetting value. The water to evaporate per mol CO2 then falls below the amount the CO2-supplying air can carry anyway, so drying stops controlling the cycle.
ideas.key_parameters: Working capacity 0.9 mol/kg (lab IRA-900 class; 0.675 effective outdoors). Wet pickup 0.4-0.6 g/g versus 3.3 g/g immersion packets (ASU 2025). Drying air 20 -> 60% RH at 20 C carries 0.383 mol H2O/m3. CO2 supply at 50% capture is 0.0087 mol/m3. Sheet thickness about 100 um, measured uptake half-time 31.8 min at 400 ppm and 30% RH. Release step 15-30 min in a closed chamber. Resin $7-54/kg. Lifetime 1,380 cycles measured outdoors (confounded) versus 15,000 needed. No purchased heat; latent heat comes from ambient air.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) Crossover: below W* = 44 mol H2O per mol CO2 (18 kg/kg), drying needs less air than CO2 supply (20 C, 20 -> 60% RH, 50% capture). (2) Immersion packet (3.3 g/g, 0.9 mol/kg): 204 mol/mol (83 kg/kg), drying air 4.6x the CO2 air, water about $125/t at $1.5/m3. Metered 0.4-0.6 g/g: 25-37 mol/mol (10-15 kg/kg), 0.6-0.8x the CO2 air, $15-23/t. Vapour wetting measured 23-24 mmol/g gives 26 mol/mol. (3) Productivity (drying then loading, kinetics floor 2 half-times plus 15 min release, 0.9 mol/kg): at 0.1 m3/s air per kg, 0.27 -> 0.46-0.48 kg CO2/kg/day; at 0.02 m3/s per kg (passive or low-fan), 0.11 -> 0.33-0.38 kg/kg/day, a 1.7-3.4x gain. Measured beads and packets are 0.19-0.27. (4) The ambient latent heat drawn falls from about 204 GJ/t to 25-37 GJ/t. It costs nothing but sets drying time. (5) Sorbent cost at 0.9 mol/kg is $12/t at $7/kg over 15,000 cycles but $988/t at $54/kg over 1,380 cycles. Wetting does not fix lifetime; it removes the water and drying penalty. Scripts: ionex_pass2.py and ionex_pass2b.py in climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/.
ideas.closest_known_work: Wang/Lackner 2011: wetting raises equilibrium CO2 pressure about 100-fold. Flory et al. 2025 (arXiv 2508.02650): immersion wetting, 330 wt% water, about 100 g water per g CO2. Sinyangwe/Wade 2026 VMS (arXiv 2606.26438): vapour wetting 23-24 mmol/g swing, 3 h. Shi/Lackner 2017: sheet kinetics. ASU moisture-swing patents (e.g. US9283510 family) mention spray wetting. No study found that maps CO2 release against metered liquid dose to find the minimum water.
ideas.why_different: Prior systems either immerse, wasting about 8x the water, or use vapour, which is slow. The proposal treats water dose as a design variable set to the resin's hydration capacity and uses a mature low-pickup applicator. The decisive release-versus-dose curve has not been published.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: 5-10 g carbonate-form resin sheets (commercial Excellion-type, or IRA-900 powder hot-pressed in PP), loaded at 400 ppm CO2, 20% RH and 25 C. In a sealed 1-2 L chamber with an NDIR logger, apply water by fine spray or foam at 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 1.0 g/g, and by full immersion. Record CO2 released over 60 min, then the drying time at 20% RH to restart uptake. Pre-stated: the idea stands if 0.6 g/g releases at least 80% of the immersion amount within 30 min and dries in no more than one-third of the immersion drying time. It is falsified if 0.6 g/g releases less than 60% of the immersion amount. Cost about $2-3k (NDIR logger, chamber, humidity generator, balance).
ideas.computational_test: Couple the Lopez-Marques/Wade IRA-900 CO2-water co-sorption isotherm to a water-activity-versus-water-content curve for the resin to predict release fraction against dose, then run a sheet-stack drying/loading model across hourly climate data to map productivity gains by site.

ideas.title: Cerium radical scavenger built into amine sorbent supports
ideas.one_line: Import the Ce3+/Ce4+ radical scavenger that extends PFSA fuel-cell membrane life by doping gamma-alumina supports with 0.25-2 wt% CeO2 under PEI. The upside is large, and one cheap TGA test settles whether it acts as an antioxidant or as a pro-oxidant.
ideas.conventional_core: PEI (Mw 800) at 35-45 wt% on gamma-Al2O3, steam- or vacuum-temperature swing at about 100 C (reference dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, q_max 2 mol/kg).
ideas.graft: Regenerative Ce3+/Ce4+ radical quenching from PEM fuel-cell membranes. There, below 0.6 wt% Ce cut voltage decay about 20-fold and fluoride emission by orders of magnitude; CeO2 is also used in hydrocarbon membranes. The Ce is placed as CeOx on the alumina pore walls, under nm-thin PEI layers, using a three-way-catalyst-type Ce-doped alumina calcined to remove nitrate.
ideas.mechanism: In fuel-cell membranes Ce3+ reduces HO* (becoming Ce4+), and Ce4+ is reduced back by HO2* or H2O2, so the ion cycles catalytically and is not consumed. In supported PEI, the films in mesopores are only a few nm thick, so any small oxygen radical or hydroperoxide made in the film is close to the doped wall. If ceria acts as on nanoceria surfaces (superoxide-dismutase- and catalase-like), it removes the HO*/H2O2 pool that Fe/Cu-Fenton chemistry feeds into chain initiation. The risk runs the opposite way: cerium carboxylates are auxiliary driers that speed hydrocarbon autoxidation, because Ce4+ can split ROOH into ROO* radicals. Which effect wins in a basic amine film at 55-120 C is unknown and cheap to measure.
ideas.key_parameters: CeO2 0.25-2 wt% of sorbent, i.e. 1.4-11 mmol Ce per mol amine N at 45 wt% PEI (10.4 mol N/kg). CeO2 at about $8/kg adds $0.02-0.16 per kg sorbent. Working capacity 1.040 -> 1.021 mol/kg (diluted). Regeneration heat 6.04 -> 6.06 GJ/t (verifier, reference cycle with 2 mol water per mol CO2). Target: at least 2-3x slower fade than control, from the 2.2e-3 %/cycle measured for engineered sorbents.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) Verifier: 0.25-2 wt% CeO2 lowers working capacity by at most 1.8% and raises regeneration heat by at most 0.02 GJ/t. (2) Cost under $0.2 per kg sorbent. (3) Value: a 3x fade reduction (2.2e-3 -> 7.3e-4 %/cycle) cuts sorbent replacement from $53 to $18/t at $20/kg and from $134 to $45/t at $50/kg. A pro-oxidant outcome (1.5x faster fade) would raise it to $80/t at $20/kg. (4) PEMFC benchmark: sub-0.6 wt% Ce reduced voltage degradation about 20x (literature, Nafion OCV tests). The bar here is set lower, at 2x, because amine autoxidation runs on carbon and peroxyl chains as well as HO*. Script: climate/runs/2026-10-06-sorbents/scripts/ionex_pass2.py.
ideas.closest_known_work: Ce and Mn scavengers in PFSA membranes (Gore/3M practice; Ce migration studies, e.g. J. Electrochem. Soc. 2016, doi 10.1149/2.0181609jes; Delaware thesis udspace.udel.edu/handle/19716/33094). CeO2 in hydrocarbon PEMs. For amine sorbents: radical-trap additives (Guta et al. 2025, PMC12703673), chelators (Min et al. 2018), metal-acceleration studies (Kuspangaliyeva 2026). Ceria has been used as a CO2 sorbent and support, but no test of ceria as an antioxidant for supported amines was found (limited search).
ideas.why_different: Organic antioxidants tested so far are consumed and block amine sites. Ce redox cycles regenerate and sit on the support rather than in the amine, so they cost under 2% of capacity. The pro-oxidant risk is named in advance, and the test discriminates the two outcomes.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Make PEI (35 wt%) on plain gamma-Al2O3 and on gamma-Al2O3 doped with 0.5 and 1 wt% CeO2 (incipient wetness, then calcined at 500 C), each with and without about 4 ppm Cu spiked into the PEI. Run three TGA protocols: (i) 18 h at 70 C in dry 0.04% CO2/air (Li 2024); (ii) 4.5 h at 120 C in dry air (Guta/Kuspangaliyeva); (iii) 30 humid cycles (adsorb 400 ppm at 50% RH and 30 C, desorb at 100 C, 20 min air at 70 C each cycle). Pre-stated: the idea stands if the Ce samples lose no more than 50% of the control's capacity loss in all three protocols, including the Cu-spiked arm, with a fresh-capacity penalty of no more than 5%. It is falsified if Ce samples lose as much as or more than the control in any protocol (no effect or pro-oxidant). Cost about $2-4k (TGA time, ICP, support doping).
ideas.computational_test: Microkinetic model of Ce3+/Ce4+ competing between HO*/HO2*/H2O2 scavenging and ROOH decomposition, using literature rate constants and the hydroperoxide levels implied by Li 2024. It predicts the sign of the Ce effect as a function of ROOH:H2O2 ratio before synthesis.

ideas.title: Red-cell carbonic anhydrase on a moisture-swing resin: speed up the slow release half-cycle
ideas.one_line: Bind carbonic anhydrase (CA), or an anionic Zn mimic, to a quaternary-ammonium moisture-swing resin. Wetting releases CO2 at about the rate of uncatalysed bicarbonate dehydration; with the catalyst, release should run as fast as the dry capture step.
ideas.conventional_core: Strong-base anion-exchange resin (IRA-900 or Purolite A501, carbonate/bicarbonate form) in a vacuum moisture swing (VMS, Wade/NAU 2026) or a passive vapour moisture swing at 25-27 C. There is no heat input.
ideas.graft: Carbonic anhydrase catalysis as used in red blood cells. CA lets bicarbonate turn into CO2 within the ~0.75 s that blood spends in a lung capillary at pH 7.4; without the enzyme this would take minutes.
ideas.mechanism: On wetting, CO2 leaves by HCO3- -> CO2 + OH- (net 2HCO3- -> CO3 2- + CO2 + H2O) at a local pH of about 8.5-10. Uncatalysed at 25 C, this proceeds at k = 2.0e-4 to 4.5e-4 /s (t1/2 26-58 min), using k_OH 8.5e3 /M/s, k_h 0.037 /s and pK1 6.35. The measured IRA-900 linear-driving-force (LDF) coefficient for wetting/release is 4.5e-4 /s, while drying/capture is 14e-4 /s (Wade 2026, TGA, 400 ppm). Release is therefore 3x slower than capture, and its rate equals the intrinsic uncatalysed dehydration rate at pH 8.5. That is consistent with the release being reaction-limited or co-limited, not only limited by water diffusion. Bovine CA II (pI ~5.9) carries a net negative charge above pH 6, so it binds electrostatically to the anion exchanger. Loading 0.1-1 mg/g gives 3-34 uM in the sorbed water. Scaling the dehydration rate by the Haldane relation from kcat/KM(hydration) 1.2e8 /M/s gives a catalysed release rate of 8e-3 to 9 /s at pH 9-10, 37x to more than 10^4x the uncatalysed rate. Release should then become limited by water and ion transport. Because CA is a catalyst, equilibrium, product pressure and water per CO2 do not change; the gain is cycle speed, i.e. capital. The graft only helps near ambient temperature: by the same constants the uncatalysed t1/2 falls to ~45 s at 60 C and ~1 s at 100 C. Moisture swing is the one DAC cycle where CA is both useful and thermally safe. Counter-evidence: Lively 2025 attributes IRA-900 kinetics to intraparticle mass transfer, and the OptiLex map predicted that CA would not help this class. The particle-size test below distinguishes the two explanations.
ideas.key_parameters: Resin: IRA-900, IEC ~4.2 mmol N+/g, 614 um beads, carbonate/bicarbonate swing ceiling ~2.1 mmol/g. Working capacity 0.9-1.1 mmol/g on a 20%->95% RH swing at 25 C, 400 ppm (measured, TGA). Binding: moisture-gated, no heat; product CO2 ~1 kPa under VMS. Catalyst: 0.1-1 mg bovine CA II per g resin (0.0003-0.003 % of IEC by charge), or a thermostable CA. Uncatalysed release t1/2 26-58 min at 25 C. Lifetime: resin cycles unchanged by the graft, enzyme life under wet/dry cycling unknown. Cost: resin $10/kg (range $7-54); enzyme assumed $50-500/kg protein.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) Intrinsic uncatalysed HCO3- -> CO2 rate at 25 C is 2.0e-4 /s (pH 10) to 4.5e-4 /s (pH 8.5); the measured release LDF of 4.5e-4 /s lies within 1-2x of it, and capture is 3.1x faster. (2) 0.1-1 mg/g CA II raises the catalysed release constant to >=8e-3 /s, so release should become transport-limited. Predicted release LDF >=1.4e-3 /s, matching drying. (3) Cycle 2 h dry + 3 h wet goes to 2 h + ~1 h: 4.8 -> 8.0 cycles/day, productivity 0.190 -> 0.317 kg CO2/kg/day (+67%), resin inventory 14.4 -> 8.6 kg per t/yr (verifier productivity(); t90 at k = 14e-4 /s is 0.46 h). (4) Energy, water per CO2 and product pressure are unchanged; VMS electricity is still the modelled ~2.5 GJ/t. (5) Enzyme cost $0.13-1.3/t CO2 at $50/kg protein, 0.1-1 mg/g, re-dosed every 1,000 cycles; $12.6/t at $500/kg and 1 mg/g. Resin cost: $84/t at $10/kg and 3,000 cycles; $17/t at 15,000 cycles (sorbent_cost_per_tonne). (6) No benefit expected at >=60 C (uncatalysed t1/2 <=45 s). Scripts: scratchpad/sorbent/bio_pass2.py (section A) and bio_pass2b.py.
ideas.closest_known_work: Wade et al., arXiv 2606.26438 (2026): VMS model with the measured IRA-900 LDF coefficients (simulation plus TGA). Wang/Realff/Lively, ACS Sustain. Chem. Eng. 2025: IRA-900 breakthrough, kinetics attributed to intraparticle mass transfer. CA immobilised on ion-exchange supports is classic enzyme immobilisation. CA has been used in liquid carbonate absorbers (CO2 Solutions/Saipem K2CO3 for flue gas; Materials 2026 CA membranes for 'enzymatic DAC', support screening only). OptiLex pass 1 put a Zn mimic in K2CO3 films, a different core. The OptiLex map explicitly predicted that CA catalysis would not help moisture-swing resins. A search found no report of CA or a CA mimic in a moisture-swing sorbent. Differences: the graft targets the release half-cycle, uses the resin's own anion-exchange sites to hold the enzyme, and exploits the fact that this is the only ambient-temperature DAC cycle.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: Step 1, no enzyme (~$500, 2 weeks): crush and sieve IRA-900 into 100-150 um and 500-600 um fractions. Run TGA at 25 C, 400 ppm CO2, 20%<->95% RH and fit LDF k for drying and for wetting. Pre-stated rule: if wetting k scales like drying k (>=5x between fractions), release is transport-limited and the idea is killed. If drying k changes >=5x but wetting k changes <2x, release is reaction-limited; go to step 2. Step 2 (~$1-2k): load 0, 0.1 and 1 mg/g bovine CA II from pH 8 buffer, dry, and repeat the TGA. Go if wetting k is >=2x the control with working capacity within +/-10%; kill if <1.3x. Step 3: 200 RH cycles; go if CA-driven acceleration retains >=50%.
ideas.computational_test: Build a bead model of gel nodules plus macropore water with temperature- and pH-dependent uncatalysed and CA-catalysed bicarbonate kinetics (constants as in bio_pass2b.py) and transport of water and ions. Fit it to the published IRA-900 drying and wetting curves (Wade 2026; Lively 2025). Test whether the 3x drying/wetting asymmetry can be reproduced without a reaction term, and predict the particle-size dependence before the experiment.
ideas.why_different: It reverses the map's negative guidance with a computed coincidence: measured release equals uncatalysed bicarbonate dehydration within 1-2x, while capture is 3x faster. It also identifies moisture swing as the only DAC cycle where an unmodified enzyme is both useful and thermally safe.

ideas.title: Ligase-like reductive re-amination: repair oxidised PEI instead of replacing it
ideas.one_line: Treat oxidised supported PEI periodically with a mild, chemoselective reductant. The imines left by C-N bond cleavage and aldehyde-amine condensation become secondary amines again, re-joining cleaved chains and restoring basic sites, as Msr enzymes and DNA ligase repair damage instead of replacing the molecule.
ideas.conventional_core: Supported branched-PEI sorbent (PEI/gamma-Al2O3 or PEI/silica, or a laminate) in steam-assisted temperature-vacuum swing at ~100 C and ~1 kPa CO2.
ideas.graft: Enzymatic self-repair. Methionine-sulfoxide reductase reduces oxidised residues back to the native state, and DNA ligase re-joins cleaved strands; damage is repaired catalytically instead of the whole molecule being replaced.
ideas.mechanism: Li et al. (JACS 2024) and Guta et al. (2023) assign PEI autoxidation products to imine and carbonyl (IR ~1660 cm-1) plus amides. Jones-group work links C-N cleavage to carbonyl species, imines and new primary amines. Each C-N cleavage turns a secondary amine into a primary amine plus an aldehyde fragment. The aldehyde condenses with a nearby amine to an imine, which is non-capturing at 420 ppm (pKa ~7), so two basic sites are lost per event. Reductive amination reduces the C=N to C-N, regenerating a basic secondary amine and covalently re-linking the fragment. Amides from the C-C cleavage route (Li 2024) are not reducible under mild conditions, so the restorable fraction rho is capped by the imine/carbonyl share of the damage. The repair would be a liquid wash of the bed (borohydride or an amine-borane reductant, <=40 C, design level only), every time ~10% capacity is lost. It is followed by a water rinse to remove borate, which would otherwise neutralise amines. A dilute-base wash control separates out capacity lost to heat-stable salts.
ideas.key_parameters: Sorbent: 40-50 wt% PEI, ~1 mol/kg working capacity, dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K, desorption 100 C at 1 kPa. Damage per repair interval: 0.1-0.3 mol/kg capacity lost, i.e. 0.2-0.6 mol imine/carbonyl sites per kg. Reductant: 3x hydride excess, 5.7-17 g NaBH4-equivalent per kg sorbent per repair ($0.11-0.68/kg at $20-40/kg). Baseline fade 20% per 5,000 cycles = 4.0e-3 %/cycle (TDA/GE measured 2.2e-3; Climeworks Gen 2 target 3.5e-3). Sorbent price $20-50/kg.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) With restorable fraction rho, effective irreversible fade = (1-rho) x baseline; rho 0.5 halves 4.0e-3 to 2.0e-3 %/cycle. (2) Sorbent replacement cost from the verifier (sorbent_cost_per_tonne, base life 5,000 cycles to 20% loss, repair reagent included). At $20/kg and wc 1.04: $87/t (no repair), $63 (rho 0.3), $46 (rho 0.5), $28 (rho 0.7). At $20/kg and wc 0.6: $152, $109, $79, $49. At $50/kg and wc 1.04: $219, $155, $111, $68. (3) Reagent per repair is <=$0.7 per kg sorbent, under 4% of a $20/kg sorbent. (4) Energy per tonne is unchanged by the graft (reference cycle 6.04 GJ/t heat), apart from the downtime of a periodic wash. Script: scratchpad/sorbent/bio_pass2.py (section C).
ideas.closest_known_work: UKCCSRC Call 2 project (University of Nottingham, ~2014) reported that thermal/oxidative degradation of PEI 'can largely be reversed' by catalytic hydrotreatment or hydrous pyrolysis below 250 C. That is a project summary only; no publication or numbers were found. Alstom/GE patent US9101912 regenerates solid amines poisoned by SO2 heat-stable salts with dilute NaOH/KOH washes, which is not oxidation. NaBH4 reduction of imines is used in synthesising crosslinked PEI sorbents. OptiLex pass 1 proposed dynamic-covalent amine refurbishment, which replaces amine. Differences: mild, in-situ, chemoselective re-joining of C-N cleavage products formed under DAC-specific oxidation (warm 400 ppm CO2 air), with a stated repair interval, a restorable-fraction bound and a price per tonne.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: ~$2-3k, about 6 weeks, TGA plus DRIFTS. Age 45 wt% PEI/gamma-Al2O3 in dry 0.04% CO2/air at 70 C until 25-35% capacity loss (literature: ~17% at 3 h; 15% after 18 h at 60 C). Split into four arms: untreated; solvent wash only; dilute KOH wash (heat-stable-salt control); reductive treatment followed by a rinse. Re-measure uptake at 400 ppm, 30 C, dry, and the 1660 cm-1 band. Go if the reductive arm recovers >=30% of the lost capacity beyond the best control arm and the 1660 band falls. Kill if recovery is <15%. Second gate: re-age the repaired sample; its fade rate must be <=1.3x that of fresh sorbent.
ideas.computational_test: Integrate a kinetic network of the published bPEI oxidation scheme (initiation, ROOH, C-N vs C-C cleavage, aldehyde-amine condensation) constrained by published capacity-loss and IR band histories (Li 2024; Guta 2023). Estimate the imine-routed share of capacity loss, which caps rho. Feed rho into sorbent_cost_per_tonne to give $/t versus repair interval.
ideas.why_different: It repairs the damaged sites rather than slowing damage (antioxidants, chelators) or replacing amine, and turns lifetime into a maintenance variable with an explicit restorable-fraction ceiling.

ideas.title: Myoglobin-style facilitated diffusion: a mobile CO2 carrier inside pore-filling PEI
ideas.one_line: Add a few wt% of a non-volatile, mobile CO2 carrier (amino-acid salt) to high-loading PEI. Bound CO2 then moves through the slow amine domains far faster than free CO2 can at 420 ppm, as myoglobin speeds O2 transport through muscle.
ideas.conventional_core: High-loading (45-55 wt%) PEI on mesoporous silica, or a laminate, in fast steam-assisted temperature-vacuum swing (20-40 min cycles).
ideas.graft: Carrier-facilitated diffusion (Scholander 1960; Wittenberg). At low ligand pressure, diffusion of myoglobin- or haemoglobin-bound O2 carries most of the flux because bound concentration greatly exceeds free concentration.
ideas.mechanism: At 420 ppm the free-CO2 concentration in the amine phase is only ~3e-5 M, against ~1-2 M bound. Flux through a PEI domain is J = (D_CO2 dC_free + D_c dq_c)/L, and the facilitation factor F = 1 + D_c q_c/(D_CO2 C_free). With D_CO2 1e-10 m2/s and a carrier with D 1e-13 to 1e-12 m2/s carrying 0.2-0.5 M, F = 18-176 at 420 ppm but only 1.1-1.7 at 10% CO2. Carbamate on polymer chains is nearly immobile. A small zwitterion/amino-acid salt loads at the domain surface and hands CO2 to empty PEI amines at the reaction front, a hand-over driven by the stronger binding of the unloaded PEI. JACS Au 2025 fits laminate-PEI uptake with an intraparticle-diffusion model, and higher PEI loading slows uptake, so transport through the amine phase limits fast-cycle capacity. Field laminates reach ~60-70% of equilibrium capacity in 20-30 min cycles.
ideas.key_parameters: PEI 45-55 wt% on silica; carrier 5-15 wt% potassium glycinate or sarcosinate (non-volatile, pKa ~9.8-10). Equilibrium capacity ~1.0 mol/kg at 400 ppm. dH -70 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K; desorption 100 C at 1 kPa. Assumed D_CO2 in PEI ~1e-10 m2/s (uncertain 1e-11 to 1e-9); carrier D 1e-13 to 1e-12 m2/s. PEI domain 1-5 um. Water swing ~3.6 mol/kg. Sorbent $20/kg.
ideas.quantitative_claims: (1) F = 18-176 at 420 ppm, 2.8-19 at 4,000 ppm, 1.1-1.7 at 10% CO2. That is the signature: the benefit should vanish at flue-gas concentration. (2) Shrinking-core time to load a 2 um domain (1.5 M bound) falls from 17.5 min (free CO2 only) to 1.8 min at F = 10 (5 um: 109 -> 11 min). (3) Raising fast-cycle use of the 1.0 mol/kg equilibrium capacity from 0.60 to 0.85 lifts productivity at 36 cycles/day from 0.95 to 1.35 kg/kg/day (+42%). With the per-kg water swing fixed and inert mass ratio 0.5, heat falls from 13.1 to 9.7 GJ/t (verifier TVSACycle at 100 C, 1 kPa; water term falls because water per CO2 drops from 6.0 to 4.2 mol/mol). (4) Sorbent $/t at $20/kg and 10,000 cycles falls from $76 to ~$54. Script: scratchpad/sorbent/bio_pass2.py (section D).
ideas.closest_known_work: Facilitated-transport membranes with mobile carriers (amino-acid salts, arginine in PVAm membranes; e.g. PMC8231264), for flue gas. PEG and surfactant additives that speed CO2 diffusion in PEI/silica. TEPA/PEI blends, where smaller amines are faster. Scholander (1960) and Wittenberg on haemoglobin- and myoglobin-facilitated O2 transport. Differences: the carrier is used inside DAC sorbent domains, and the idea makes a quantitative, falsifiable prediction that the benefit grows as pCO2 falls (large at 420 ppm, ~nil at 10%), which separates facilitated diffusion from plain plasticisation.
ideas.cheapest_falsifying_test: ~$1-2k, TGA, 4-6 weeks. Make 50 wt% PEI/silica with 0, 5 and 10 wt% K-glycinate replacing equal PEI mass. Record uptake curves at 25 C, both dry and 50% RH, at 400 ppm and at 10% CO2. Pre-stated rule: go if t50 at 400 ppm falls >=2x while the t50 ratio at 10% CO2 stays <=1.3x and equilibrium capacity falls <=10%. Kill if the 400 ppm improvement is <1.3x, or if it is equally large at 10% CO2 (then it is only plasticisation, not facilitation). Also require <1% mass loss in 10 h at 100 C under N2 (carrier non-volatile).
ideas.computational_test: Build a 1D reaction-diffusion slab model with free CO2, PEI Langmuir sites and a mobile carrier, and fit D_CO2 to published 400 ppm uptake curves of 40-50 wt% PEI/silica (JACS Au 2025 intraparticle-diffusion constants). Predict t50 versus carrier D and loading at 420 ppm, 4,000 ppm and 10%; this fixes the carrier D needed for a 2x speed-up before any synthesis.
ideas.why_different: It targets the slow amine-phase transport behind fast-cycle under-utilisation with a mechanism whose advantage grows exactly as CO2 becomes more dilute, which is DAC's defining condition.

ideas.title: RuBisCO-style Mg2+-stabilised carbamate to rescue oxidation-resistant amines
ideas.one_line: Dope epoxide-functionalised (oxidation-resistant but too weakly binding) PEI with redox-inert Mg2+. Mg2+ pairs with the carbamate, as in RuBisCO Lys201 carbamylation, and should restore the ~4 kJ/mol the stabilisation removed.
ideas.conventional_core: Epoxybutane-functionalised PEI on silica (Min et al. 2018 type, about 50x slower oxidative deactivation with a chelator) in temperature-vacuum swing at 90-100 C and 1 kPa.
ideas.graft: Metal-assisted carbamylation in RuBisCO. The Lys201 epsilon-amine binds an activator CO2 as a carbamate that becomes stable at physiological pH only when Mg2+ coordinates it; the cation pays part of the free energy.
ideas.mechanism: Epoxide functionalisation hydrogen-bonds and immobilises the amines and slows radical oxidation, but it lowers the heat of adsorption from 80.5 to 66.2 kJ/mol (Min 2018, flue-gas pressure). In the verifier (dS -165) a -66 kJ/mol site is only 27% filled at 420 ppm and gives 0.46 mol/kg. A divalent, redox-inert Mg2+ (no Fenton chemistry, unlike Cu or Fe) can replace the ammonium partner of the carbamate ion pair with a contact Mg-O2CNR pair. Diamine-Mg2(dobpdc) shows such Mg-carbamates form at DAC strength. Only -3 to -6 kJ/mol of extra free energy is needed; overshooting (-8) pushes the regeneration temperature to 113 C. Mg is dosed at ~1 per 2 target carbamates with a weakly coordinating, non-oxidising anion such as acetate; nitrates are avoided because of the oxidiser hazard. Main risk: hydration of Mg2+ in humid air may screen the pairing, as water erases cooperativity in diamine MOFs; the test is run at 50% RH for that reason.
ideas.key_parameters: Base site dH -66 kJ/mol, dS -165 J/mol/K. Target ddG -3 to -6 kJ/mol. Mg 0.1-0.3 mol/kg (2.4-7 g Mg/kg; ~54 g Mg acetate tetrahydrate per kg at 0.25 mol/kg, ~$0.11/kg). Adsorption 25 C, 400 ppm, dry and 50% RH; desorption 90-100 C at 1 kPa with 2 mol water per CO2. Lifetime: retain the epoxide-PEI oxidation advantage (target <=1.2x its fade). Sorbent $20/kg.
ideas.quantitative_claims: Verifier figures at q_max 2 mol/kg, 100 C, 1 kPa, 2 H2O/CO2: (1) The -66 kJ/mol site gives 27% fill, wc 0.46 mol/kg, 9.0 GJ/t heat, $98/t sorbent at $20/kg and 10,000 cycles. (2) ddG -4 kJ/mol (enthalpic) gives 65% fill, wc 1.04, 6.04 GJ/t, work-equivalent 1.88, $44/t. ddG -6 gives wc 1.17, 5.82 GJ/t, T_des 102 C. ddG -8 overshoots (90% fill, T_des 113 C, wc 1.10). (3) If the -4 kJ/mol bonus is partly entropic (ddH -10/ddS -20 or ddH -16/ddS -40), T_des(20% residual, 1 kPa) falls to 86/80 C and wc rises to 1.14/1.20 mol/kg at ~5.98 GJ/t. (4) Dopant cost ~$0.1 per kg sorbent. Scripts: scratchpad/sorbent/bio_pass2.py (section E) and bio_pass2b.py.
